title: Timing of platelet-rich plasma administration in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated as a biologic adjunct in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR), yet clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. One potential source of variability is the timing of PRP administration, which may influence tendon-to-bone healing. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of PRP augmentation on structural healing and clinical outcomes following ARCR, with particular evaluation of outcomes according to the timing of PRP administration.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL and Web of Science were searched through 19 February 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PRP augmentation with control in adult patients undergoing ARCR were included. Trials were stratified by timing of PRP administration (intraoperative, post-operative-only or combined). The primary outcome was retears assessed by post-operative imaging at ≥6 months. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics.
RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs (1214 patients; 647 PRP and 567 control) met inclusion criteria. Overall, PRP administration at ≥6 months was associated with a reduced risk of retears (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that intraoperative PRP significantly reduced retear rates at ≥6 months (RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.35-0.68; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%) and ≥12 months (RR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.30-0.91; p = 0.021; I2 = 0%). Post-operative-only PRP did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in retears (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.01-8.12; p = 0.54). Absolute risk reduction at ≥6 months was approximately 12%, corresponding to a number needed to treat of 8. Functional outcome scores improved in both PRP and control groups, with significant differences between groups in included studies, but pooled analyses did not demonstrate consistent between-group differences. PRP was not associated with increased complication rates.
CONCLUSION: Intraoperative PRP augmentation during ARCR is associated with a statistically significant reduction in retears. The limited post-operative-only PRP protocols do not demonstrate a comparable benefit and preclude a definitive conclusion that efficacy differs according to timing. These findings suggest a potential timing-dependent structural effect of PRP. However, structural improvements did not consistently translate into superior functional outcomes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.
journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA

title: Prestroke and Poststroke Physical Activity and Depression, Anxiety, and Fatigue After Ischemic Stroke: A Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Depression, anxiety, and fatigue are common and disabling long-term sequelae of stroke. Whether habitual physical activity before stroke and engagement in physical activity during recovery are associated with poststroke psychological outcomes remains incompletely understood. We investigated associations between physical activity patterns and psychological outcomes during the first year after ischemic stroke.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, consecutive patients with ischemic stroke enrolled in the STROKE-CARD Registry were assessed for depression, anxiety, and fatigue at either 3- or 12-month follow-up after stroke using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale and Fatigue Severity Scale. Physical activity was assessed before and after stroke with the Baecke Questionnaire. Associations between physical activity and psychological outcomes were assessed using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, prestroke and poststroke disability, stroke severity and localization, thrombolysis, prestroke depression, and cognitive impairment.
RESULTS: Within 1050 patients (median age, 70 years; 35% female), 35.3% were screened positive for depression, 29.9% for anxiety, and 53.2% for fatigue at either 3 or 12 months after stroke. Both prestroke and poststroke physical activity were associated with lower odds of depression (adjusted odds ratio, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.36-0.62] and 0.45 [95% CI, 0.34-0.59]; P<0.001) and fatigue (adjusted odds ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.38-0.64] and 0.49 [95% CI, 0.38-0.64]; P<0.001), and with lower odds of anxiety (adjusted odds ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.57-1.00]; P=0.050) and (adjusted odds ratio, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.53-0.94]; P=0.016). High-intensity and high-volume activities were associated with the lowest prevalence of depression and fatigue (depression, 24.5%-25.7%; fatigue, 40.8%-44.1%). Endurance sports were associated with lower rates of depression (22.2%; P<0.001) and fatigue (40.6%; P<0.001), whereas strength training was associated with lower anxiety (12.8%; P=0.003).
CONCLUSIONS: Physical activity before and after stroke was associated with lower odds of depression, anxiety, and fatigue. These findings identify physical activity as a potentially modifiable behavioral factor associated with psychological well-being after stroke and support further evaluation in intervention studies.

title: Comparative Effects of Different Neuromuscular Training Modalities and Doses on Lower-Limb Injury Prevention in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lower-limb injuries are common in athletes. Neuromuscular training (NMT) is widely promoted, but the comparative effectiveness of different modalities and the optimal dose remain uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a PRISMA-compliant, PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library and Embase were searched to 1 August 2025. Eligible trials compared NMT with a control in athletes and reported lower-limb injury outcomes. Random-effects models pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Two reviewers screened, extracted and assessed risk of bias. Prespecified subgroups examined modality and dose (frequency, session duration, intervention length), age, sex and sport. Certainty was rated with GRADE.
RESULTS: Twenty-seven RCTs (27,663 participants) were included. NMT was associated with reduced lower-limb injury risk (RR = 0.72, 95% CI 0.64-0.82), although trim-and-fill adjustment attenuated the estimate. Structured (RR = 0.68, 95% CI 0.56-0.82) and multidimensional programmes (RR = 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.93) showed favourable pooled estimates, with no statistically significant between-modality difference. Favourable pooled estimates were also observed in adolescents (RR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.81) and young adults (RR = 0.70, 95% CI 0.50-0.99), and in football (RR = 0.71) and basketball (RR = 0.66); however, the between-age difference did not remain statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, and no statistically significant differences were detected between sport subgroups. Low-certainty, study-level subgroup analyses yielded favourable pooled estimates for programmes delivered 2-3 times per week, for 16-25 min per session, and over intervention periods of 1.5-12 months; however, these associations did not establish a causal or optimal dose. Certainty was very low overall and low to very low across dosage comparisons.
CONCLUSIONS: NMT may reduce lower-limb injury risk, but the magnitude of benefit remains very uncertain. Structured and multidimensional programmes, together with programmes delivered at moderate frequency and duration, showed favourable pooled estimates in exploratory subgroup analyses; however, the dose-related findings represent study-level associations and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal or optimal dose. These findings may inform the design of routine training programmes, while future high-quality RCTs should address adherence, long-term sustainability, and dose-response interactions across sports and populations.

title: Maximal Aerobic Capacity and Aging in Female Masters Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Maximal aerobic capacity ( V ˙ O2max) represents the highest rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense exercise and is a key determinant of endurance performance. Although age-related declines in V ˙ O2max have been well documented in male individuals, less is known about this trajectory in female Masters athletes, defined as individuals aged 40 years or older who often engage in lifelong endurance training.
OBJECTIVE: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify cross-sectional age-related differences in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes.
METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 14 May, 2025 for studies reporting directly measured V ˙ O2max in female Masters endurance athletes aged 40 years or older. Eligible exercise modalities included running, cycling, swimming, and large muscle-mass ergometry, with testing conducted under standard environmental conditions. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using a modified Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled mean V ˙ O2max values were calculated for predefined age groups (40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70 years or older) using a random-effects meta-analysis. Meta-regression was used to estimate the relationship between age and V ˙ O2max.
RESULTS: Sixty-nine studies, including 1903 female Masters athletes, met the inclusion criteria. Pooled mean relative V ˙ O2max was 45 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 43.0-46.8) in athletes aged 40-49 years, 40 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 38.5-41.7) in those aged 50-59 years, 35 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 33.2-37.1) in those aged 60-69 years, and 30 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 27.2-31.8) in athletes aged 70 years or older. Meta-regression demonstrated that each additional year of age was associated with a 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 lower V ˙ O2max (95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.44; P < 0.0001), equivalent to about 11.7% per decade. The association was consistent across testing modalities.
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates a progressive age-related decrease in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. Maximal aerobic capacity declines at an average rate of 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 per year after age 40 years, corresponding to approximately 11.7% per decade. This decline is evident across endurance sport disciplines and appears consistent with physiological changes associated with aging despite sustained endurance training. These findings provide female-specific reference values and a quantitative framework for future studies on aerobic capacity trajectories in female athletes.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S2RXZ ).

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Relationship between global functional outcomes and patient-reported instability after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction: A midterm case series of 292 patients.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate midterm patient-reported outcomes, return to sport (RTS) rates and instability-specific symptoms after arthroscopic anatomic lateral ankle ligament reconstruction (AALALR), and to evaluate the relationship between global functional recovery and perceived ankle stability.
METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 292 patients who underwent AALALR between January 2015 and May 2022, with a mean follow-up of 4.9 ± 1.8 years. Global outcomes were assessed using the foot and ankle ability measure (FAAM) and simple ankle value (SAV), while instability-specific perception was evaluated with the French Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT-F). RTS, satisfaction and complications were also recorded. No objective postoperative laxity assessment was performed.
RESULTS: Mean FAAM-ADL was 94.3 ± 12.0, FAAM-Sports 87.5 ± 20.4 and SAV 85.1 ± 17.4; 89.7% of patients returned to sport and 91.1% were satisfied. Overall, 104 patients (35.6%; 95% CI, 30.3-41.3) met the CAIT-F criterion for instability at follow-up (score ≤23/30). Patients with CAIT-F-defined instability had significantly lower FAAM and SAV scores and RTS rates (all p < 0.001), although most had returned to sport (79.8%) and were satisfied (81.7%). The CAIT-F correlated moderately with FAAM-activities of daily living (ADL), FAAM-Sports and SAV (Spearman ρ = 0.68-0.69) and receiver operating characteristic analysis showed imperfect agreement between global scores and CAIT-F-defined categories (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.82-0.85). The reoperation rate was 5.5%.
CONCLUSION: AALALR provides high midterm satisfaction, favourable functional scores and favourable RTS rates. However, over one-third of patients reported current CAIT-F-defined instability symptoms. Global and instability-specific instruments are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable, and prospective studies including objective laxity assessment are needed.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women.
CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Most National Football League Players Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Repair, Yet Only One-Half Regain Preinjury Performance With Persistent Pass-Rush Decline at Year 2.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate National Football League (NFL) player performance using advanced statistics after Achilles tendon (AT) repair.
METHODS: NFL players who underwent AT repair between 2017 and 2023 were identified from a publicly available injury database. Demographic and performance data were collected preinjury and up to 2 seasons postinjury, with a minimum follow-up of 1 regular-season game required to assess return to play (RTP). RTP was defined as being active for a regular-season game and return to performance as achieving ≥90% of preinjury performance. Performance was assessed using Sports Information Solutions' points above replacement (PAR). Factors associated with RTP and return to performance were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with pre- and postinjury performance compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate.
RESULTS: Seventy-seven NFL players with AT repairs were identified. Ten were excluded for no prior regular-season play, leaving 67 included. Overall, 77.6% (n = 52) returned to play. Increasing age reduced the odds of RTP (odds ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval [0.60-0.95], P = .02). Index games preinjury increased the odds of RTP (odds ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval [1.01-1.24], P = .04). Body mass index, position, index games played, and index PAR were not significant. Among returnees, 50% (n = 26) achieved at least 90% of preinjury performance. Higher index PAR predicted lower odds of meeting this threshold (odds ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval [0.66-0.90], P = .00). Pass-rush PAR declined at year 2 after injury from 1.17 (±5.19) preinjury to -0.66 (±2.15), P = .02.
CONCLUSIONS: In this study using publicly available data, 77.6% of NFL players returned to play after AT repair; however, only one-half of these players regained ≥90% of their preinjury performance. Older age reduced the likelihood of RTP, whereas more preinjury games started increased it. Higher preinjury PAR reduced the likelihood of performance recovery. Pass-rush performance declined by the second postinjury season.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective therapeutic case series.

title: Effects of repeated isometric exercise on pain-related and physical recovery outcomes following exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate repeated quadriceps isometric exercise for recovery following experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes.
DESIGN: Parallel-group, randomized sham-controlled trial.
METHODS: Forty university athletes were randomized to isometric exercise (n = 20) or sham exercise (n = 20). Co-primary outcomes were pressure pain threshold and soreness intensity; secondary outcomes were knee flexion range of motion, quadriceps isometric strength, and thigh circumference. Assessments occurred before and immediately after soreness induction and on Days 1, 3, and 5. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for soreness (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.898), pressure pain threshold (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.745), and knee flexion range of motion (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.378). Soreness was lower in the isometric group on Day 1 (mean difference, -2.55 points; 95% confidence interval -3.00 to -2.10; Hedges' g = -3.19) and Day 3 (-1.90 points; 95% confidence interval -2.35 to -1.45; Hedges' g = -2.74). Pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed no significant between-group differences at individual time points. Group × Time interactions were not significant for quadriceps strength or thigh circumference.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated submaximal isometric exercise was associated with lower perceived soreness during peak symptoms. Although pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed different temporal patterns, neither differed significantly between groups at individual time points. Benefits for physical recovery outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Limitations of Rotational Acceleration for Predicting Concussion: A New Injury Risk Function.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Rotational acceleration of the head has long been hypothesized to be a primary driver of concussion because it can generate shear strains in brain tissue, while linear acceleration has been considered less injurious due to the brain's near-incompressibility. Instrumented mouthguards (iMGs) now enable direct six-degree-of-freedom measurements of human concussion, making it possible to rigorously test this hypothesis for the first time in vivo. The purpose of this study was to test the hypothesis that rotational acceleration is a more precise predictor of concussion than linear acceleration using iMG measurements of concussion across a multi-sport dataset.
METHODS: A dataset of 47 concussive and 3,804 non-concussive iMG-measured impacts was compiled across male and female athletes in seven sports. Univariate and bivariate logistic regression models were developed using peak linear acceleration, peak rotational acceleration, and peak rotational velocity to assess concussion classification and contribution to injury risk. Models were evaluated using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), F1 score, and odds ratios. Additionally, a novel liquid-filled helmet technology was evaluated during laboratory impacts using the derived risk functions.
RESULTS: Contrary to our hypothesis, rotational acceleration was not a significantly more precise classifier than linear acceleration (AUPRC = 0.36 vs 0.65; F1 = 0.31 vs 0.50) and was not a significant independent predictor of concussion alongside linear acceleration in a bivariate model (ORrot = 1.3, 95% CI 0.81-1.9; ORlin = 2.3; 95% CI 1.5-3.6). However, peak rotational velocity provided additional predictive value in a bivariate risk function with peak linear acceleration. Applying this bivariate function to laboratory football helmet tests, the liquid-filled padding reduced predicted concussion risk by up to 60% relative to a standard American football helmet, primarily due to attenuating linear acceleration.
CONCLUSION: Rotational acceleration was not a significant independent predictor of concussion and was outperformed by linear acceleration in classification, challenging its primacy in injury risk evaluation. Our results support a broader consideration of linear acceleration and rotational velocity in concussion risk assessment and prevention.

title: Interval Between Injury and Surgery Influences Knee Biomechanics During Walking in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstructed Patients: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is commonly performed to restore anatomical and functional knee stability. Although altered walking biomechanics have been observed post-ACLR, previous studies have not consistently accounted for the interval between injury and surgery.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine whether walking-related knee biomechanical alterations following ACLR are transient or persist over time, and whether the timing of surgery influences these alterations.
METHODS: Five electronic databases (Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, Physiotherapy Evidence Database [PEDro], and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [CENTRAL]) were systematically searched from inception through August 2026. Studies comparing walking biomechanics between patients who underwent ACLR and healthy controls and reporting the interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and reconstructive surgery were included. Biomechanical outcomes during the stance phase of walking were extracted and stratified according to the interval between injury and surgery: short term (0 to < 6 months), mid-term (6 to < 12 months), and long term (≥ 12 months). Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using a random-effects model. Study quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist.
RESULTS: Of the 3522 identified records, 16 studies involving male and female participants aged 18-55 years met the inclusion criteria. The mean methodological quality score was 65%, indicating an overall moderate level of methodological quality. Compared with healthy controls, ACLR participants demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] - 0.64 to - 0.02, p = 0.03, I2 = 57%), peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.47, 95% CI - 0.92 to - 0.01, p = 0.04, I2 = 66%), and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 0.64, 95% CI - 1.05 to - 0.23, p = 0.002, I2 = 76%). In subgroup analyses, the long-term group (≥ 12 months between injury and surgery) demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.27, 95% CI - 0.54 to - 0.00, p = 0.05, I2 = 8%) and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 1.97, 95% CI - 3.77 to - 0.17, p = 0.03, I2 = 88%). The short-term group (0 to < 6 months) demonstrated lower peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.79, 95% CI - 1.18 to - 0.40, p < 0.0001, I2 = 19%) and peak knee extension moment (SMD = - 0.55, 95% CI - 0.93 to - 0.18, p = 0.004, I2 = 50%).
CONCLUSIONS: The interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and ACLR was associated with differences in postoperative walking biomechanics. Delayed reconstruction (≥ 12 months) is associated with persistent sagittal plane deficits, which may reflect chronic neuromuscular adaptations or preoperative joint degeneration. In contrast, early surgery (within 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament injury) was associated with fewer long-term sagittal-plane deficits, although temporary frontal-plane asymmetries and extension deficits may persist during the early postoperative period and may improve with rehabilitation. These findings underscore the importance of considering the timing of ACLR when planning surgery and postoperative rehabilitation to support walking recovery.

title: Recovery of Running and Technical Match Performance After Adductor Muscle Strain Injury in Male Professional Football Players: A Prospective Cohort Study of 27 Players From One LaLiga Team Across Five Seasons.
abstract: Post return-to-play (RTP) running and technical match performance after adductor muscle strain injury remains unclear. The aim of the present study was to examine recovery of running and technical match performance after RTP following acute adductor muscle strain injury in professional football. This prospective longitudinal cohort study followed players from one team (n = 122) across five seasons (2020/2021-2024/2025). Injuries were recorded by the medical staff and confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging. Match performance variables included playing time, total distance, high-speed running distance (> 24 km/h), number of sprints (> 24 km/h), and offensive and defensive technical actions. First eight matches following RTP were compared with the four pre-injury matches. RTP required unrestricted team training and medical clearance for match selection. Data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations methods, adjusting event counts for the amount of playing time. Of the 122 players, 27 sustained at least one acute adductor muscle strain injury, accounting for 54 injury episodes. At Match 1, time played was -7.1% versus PRE (95% CI -16.7% to +3.5%), total-distance rate -0.4% (-2.4% to +1.5%), high-speed running distance +6.9% (-3.5% to +18.5%), and number of sprints +5.9% (-4.0% to +16.8%); none remained significant after FDR adjustment (p ≥ 0.182; pFDR ≥ 0.817). At Match 8, total passes were 26.5% below PRE (95% CI -50.0% to +7.9%; raw p = 0.116; pFDR = 0.567). Across all Match 1-8 contrasts, only long passes at Match 3 remained significant after FDR adjustment (-15.3%; 95% CI -22.4% to -7.6%; raw p < 0.001; pFDR = 0.022). In conclusion, there was little evidence of systematic population-level impairment in running or technical match performance after RTP. Late passing reductions warrant confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

title: Stress Fracture Recovery and Return to Sports in Youth with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare stress fracture recovery times in children with and without juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), and to evaluate JIA-related factors associated with recovery.
STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective case-control study included children with JIA <19 years old with a first stress fracture treated at a single center from 2004-2024. Cases were matched 1:3 to children without JIA by age, gender, and fracture location. Recovery time was defined from imaging confirmation of a stress fracture to medical clearance to return to sports. We used a generalized estimating equations method to compare recovery times and evaluate associations with JIA-related factors, including JIA subtype, glucocorticoid and arthritis-directed therapy exposure, and proximity of arthritis to fracture location.
RESULTS: The cohort included 260 children (65 cases, 195 controls; 53.8% female; median age 14.3 years [IQR 12.6, 16.2]). Pars interarticularis fractures accounted for 30.8% of injuries, followed by metatarsal (23.1%), and tibial fractures (14.2%). Among children with JIA who sustained pars fractures, 75.0% had an enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) phenotype. Median recovery times were 10.6 (IQR 7.0, 19.4) weeks for children with JIA and 10.6 (IQR 7.1, 14.6) weeks for controls (P=0.197), with no significant differences for lower-extremity fractures. In contrast, children with JIA who sustained pars fractures had longer recovery times than controls (ratio of geometric means: 1.44, 95% CI 1.01, 2.05; P=0.045). Among children with active sacroiliitis, fractures occurred more frequently in the proximate pars or pelvis than at non-proximate sites (P<0.001). Recovery time was not associated with JIA subtype (all p>0.150), glucocorticoid exposure (P=0.365), or biologic therapy (P=0.625).
CONCLUSIONS: Overall recovery times did not differ significantly between children with and without JIA. However, children with JIA and pars fractures had longer recovery times, and associations with ERA and sacroiliitis warrant further investigation. Additional research on spondylolysis recovery in young athletes with JIA may help inform individualized return-to-sports recommendations.

title: Bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with a higher 1-year risk of thigh muscle injury after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in competitive male athletes: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft type and subsequent thigh muscle injury in athletes involved in pivoting sports.
METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 221 ACLRs performed in 199 competitive male athletes involved in pivoting sports, classified according to graft donor site: extensor mechanism (bone-patellar tendon-bone [BPTB] or quadriceps tendon) and flexor mechanism (hamstring tendon). Only athletes who returned to sport and completed a minimum of 12 months of follow-up were included. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-confirmed thigh muscle injuries occurring within the first year following the discharge date were identified and classified by muscle group injured and graft type.
RESULTS: Thirty-five athletes (15.8%) sustained at least one MRI-confirmed thigh muscle injury (41 muscle-group-level injuries in total) in the year after discharge from ACLR. Athletes who received a graft from the extensor mechanism had a higher proportion of any thigh muscle injury than those with hamstring grafts (27/133, 20.3% vs. 8/88, 9.1%; absolute risk difference 11.2%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.4-20.0; odds ratio [OR] 2.45, 95% CI 1.12-5.88; p = 0.037). Muscle-group analyses showed no significant differences for hamstring injury or quadriceps injury. All six adductor injuries occurred in the extensor donor group (4.5% vs. 0%), but this difference was not statistically robust. After adjustment, none of the three muscle-group comparisons remained significant.
CONCLUSION: Extensor mechanism grafts were associated with a higher proportion of athletes sustaining any thigh muscle injury in the year following discharge from rehabilitation; although absolute rates were low, no individual muscle group showed a significant difference.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Long-term market value decline after medial collateral ligament injury in professional football players did not differ statistically significantly from matched non-injured controls: A Transfermarkt-based cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to characterize the longitudinal trajectory of estimated market value after medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury in professional football players and determine whether postinjury changes differed from matched non-injured controls.
METHODS: Professional football players with a recorded MCL injury were identified from Transfermarkt injury records labeled as medial (collateral) ligament injuries (seasons 2007/08-2023/24); duplicate records of the same episode were merged, and injuries were not clinically verified. Market value was assessed during the season preceding injury (Tpre), the injury season (T0), and annually for five subsequent seasons (T1-T5). Linear mixed-effect models evaluated longitudinal changes and associations with age, playing position, league level, and injury-related absence. Segmented models assessed changes in temporal trajectory. MCL cases were also matched 1:2 to non-injured controls by competition, season, playing position, age, and preinjury market value, with group differences examined using a difference-in-differences model.
RESULTS: Forty-five players with 50 MCL injury episodes were included, 8 of which had an associated anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal lesion. Median age at injury was 26.5 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 23.0-28.7), and median time lost was 42 days (IQR: 21-76.5). In the adjusted model, market value did not differ statistically significantly from Tpre at T0 (P = 0.649), T1 (P = 0.813), or T2 (P = 0.064) but was statistically significantly lower at T3 (-34.25%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -51.21% to -11.38%; P = 0.006), T4 (-47.54%; 95% CI: -61.54% to -28.43%; P < 0.001), and T5 (-51.70%; 95% CI: -65.25% to -32.88%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant postinjury change in slope was observed (P = 0.103). Thirty-one of 48 eligible cases were matched to 62 controls; the remaining 17 had no eligible control within the matching criteria, mostly because of lower-tier competition or low preinjury market value. Difference-in-differences estimates were not statistically significant at any time point (P = 0.167-0.561; range: -10.9% [95% CI: -39.2% to 30.6%] at T0 to -24.6% [95% CI: -49.5% to 12.6%] at T3); the study could detect only differences of approximately 42%-46% or more. Results were unchanged when analyses were restricted to isolated MCL injuries.
CONCLUSIONS: Market value declined substantially during long-term follow-up after MCL injury, but this decline was not statistically significantly different from that observed in matched non-injured players (P = 0.167-0.561). Much of the apparent long-term depreciation may therefore reflect the underlying age- and career-related trajectory of professional footballers; however, the matched analysis was underpowered, and a modest injury-specific effect, particularly after more severe injuries with longer absence, cannot be excluded. Because injury grade and treatment were unavailable, these findings should not be generalized to high-grade or operatively treated MCL injuries.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: University athletes face substantial academic, physical, and psychosocial pressures that may heighten vulnerability to psychological distress, despite the perceived mental health benefits of sports participation. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh and to examine how these conditions are associated with lifestyle and sociodemographic factors.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to September 2025 among 249 university athletes aged 18-26 years at six randomly selected universities in Bangladesh. Data were collected online and in person. Psychological distress was assessed with the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and health-promoting lifestyle behaviors were evaluated with the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP-II). Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's correlations, and binary logistic regression analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: The prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress was 42.6%, 42.6%, and 43.8%, respectively. Depression, anxiety, and stress were significantly associated with relationship status, fatigue, socioeconomic status, smoking, sleep duration, sports participation frequency, and satisfaction with sports (all p < 0.05). Participants with depression, anxiety, and stress had significantly lower scores across all HPLP-II domains (all p < 0.01). Higher physical activity was independently associated with lower odds of depression (OR = 0.462, 95% CI: 0.286-0.746), anxiety (OR = 0.756, 95% CI: 0.677-0.845), and stress (OR = 0.773, 95% CI: 0.677-0.882). Better stress management and stronger interpersonal relationships were also significantly associated, whereas other factors were not.
CONCLUSIONS: Depression, anxiety, and stress were highly prevalent among university athletes in Bangladesh and strongly associated with modifiable lifestyle factors. These findings support integrated, athlete-centered mental health strategies emphasizing physical activity, stress management, and psychosocial support. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and determination of the directionality of these associations.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Global Positioning System-Derived Match Demands and Their Association With On-Field Technical Performance in Elite Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) Athletes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study sought to determine the associations between global positioning system-derived match demands and technical performance in elite Australian Football League Women's athletes.
METHODS: Global positioning system match demands (total distance, speed, acceleration, high-intensity running [>19 km·h-1], very high-intensity running [>21 km·h-1], sprint distances [>24 km·h-1]) were measured with Catapult Vector S7 global positioning system units during the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes for each game were considered technical performance outcomes. Linear mixed effects regression models examined associations between match demands and technical performance, adjusting for season, ground location, and playing position.
RESULTS: Five hundred sixty-six player match profiles from 32 athletes across the 2 seasons were analyzed. Ranking points were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .29 [95% CI .22-.40]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.15]), and acceleration (R2 = .09 [.00-.23]). Best and fairest votes were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .23 [.17-.34]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.11]), acceleration (R2 = .05 [.00-.17]), and very high-intensity running distance per minute (R2 = .00 [.00-.13]).
CONCLUSIONS: Total distance, speed, acceleration, and very high-intensity running distance per minute were associated with Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes across Australian Football League Women's seasons 2023 and 2024. This suggests that athletes who cover greater total distances and achieve higher average acceleration get more opportunities to be involved in match-play and demonstrate higher levels of technical performance.

title: Comparative physiological responses to self-paced exercise in men across age-training status: effort distribution, cerebral-muscle oxygenation and neuromuscular performance.
abstract: To compare self-paced cycling performance, effort distribution, and associated neuromuscular and physiological responses across three age-training phenotypes. Twenty-eight healthy men were classified as young trained (YT, n = 8; 26.3 ± 6.9 y), older trained (OT, n = 11; 57.5 ± 3.4 y), or young untrained (YU, n = 9; 24.8 ± 5.3 y). Participants completed a 25-min self-paced cycling time trial comprising five 4.5-min lower-intensity sections, each followed by a 30-s maximal sprint. Power output, heart rate (HR), rating of perceived exertion, blood lactate, core and skin temperature, cerebral and muscle tissue oxygenation, and pre/post knee-extensor neuromuscular function were assessed. Total distance differed between groups (P = 0.037), with OT cycling further than YU (12.87 ± 1.32 vs. 11.48 ± 0.89 km; mean difference 1.40 km, 95% CI 0.35-2.44; adjusted P = 0.035), whereas OT and YT did not differ. During lower-intensity sections, OT produced greater absolute power than YU (mean difference 51.8 W, 95% CI 18.8-84.7; adjusted P = 0.012). Sprint-power variability was lower in OT than YU (7.8 ± 6.0 vs. 28.4 ± 18.5%; adjusted P = 0.030). Peak HR was lower in OT than both younger groups. Voluntary activation showed no significant group x time interaction (P = 0.062), and NIRS responses showed no significant group x stage interactions. Older trained men achieved self-paced cycling performance comparable with young trained men and greater than young untrained men, characterised by sustained lower-intensity power and more stable sprint output despite a lower peak HR.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient.
METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only.
RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses.
CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

title: The role of scapular muscles strengthening in lateral epicondylalgia rehabilitation: A systematic review with meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lateral epicondylalgia is a prevalent tendinopathy often recurring despite conventional physiotherapy. Emerging evidence suggests that scapular muscles strengthening improves outcomes by addressing proximal kinetic chain deficits.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of scapular muscles strengthening combined with conventional physiotherapy compared with conventional physiotherapy alone in patients with Lateral epicondylalgia.
STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, PEDro, Scopus, Web of Science and ScienceDirect were searched up to January 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized experimental studies with Lateral Epicondylalgia were included. Outcomes were pain (Visual Analog Scale, Numeric Pain Rating Scale), grip strength (dynamometer), and function {pain and disability (Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation)}. Methodological quality was assessed using Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) appraisal tool. Risk of bias was evaluated using Revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for Randomized Trials and Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of interventions, and certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
RESULTS: Twelve studies [10 RCTs, 2 non-randomized) were included, with 8 RCTs pooled for meta-analysis. Scapular muscles strengthening plus conventional therapy demonstrated significant functional improvement (PRTEE: MD = -9.33; 95% CI -15.01 to -3.65; p = 0.001; I² = 73%). No significant pooled effect was found for pain (SMD = -0.36; 95% CI -1.24-0.52; p = 0.43; I² = 86%) or grip strength (SMD = 0.19; 95% CI -0.09-0.47; p = 0.18). Overall low to moderate risk of bias, with good RCTs quality (PEDro mean score=6/10) and high non- RCTs quality (JBI). Overall certainty of evidence was moderate for pain and grip strength and low for PRTEE.
CONCLUSION: Scapular muscles strengthening combined with conventional physiotherapy provides superior functional outcomes compared with conventional therapy alone in patients with LE. Effects on pain and grip strength remain inconclusive.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers.
METHODS: Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery.
RESULTS: Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences.
CONCLUSION: Black chokeberry supplementation may influence markers related to short-term post-exercise iron availability, potentially in association with inflammatory and antioxidant responses, without detectable effects on body iron stores or erythropoiesis.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06486623; registration date: 2024-07-03).

title: Patients treated with rehabilitation alone after anterior cruciate ligament injury display greater muscle strength symmetry, yet lower absolute muscle strength normalized to bodyweight compared to reconstruction: A Cross-sectional study of 3,093 patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Younger patients active at a greater activity level are in general treated with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) while older, less active patients receive rehabilitation alone as primary treatment. Objective of this study was to compare muscle strength, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) between patients treated with rehabilitation alone and rehabilitation with additional ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during the first 12 months after treatment.
DESIGN: Registry-based cohort study.
SETTING: Cross-sectional comparisons adjusted for age and sex using ANCOVA.
PARTICIPANTS: 3093 patients (2707 ACLR; 386 rehabilitation), aged ≥15 years and registered in Project ACL.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Muscle strength and PROs assessed at 10 weeks, 4, 8, and 12 months after ACL injury or ACLR.
RESULTS: In the comparison between patients treated with rehabilitation alone and ACLR, patients in the rehabilitation alone group had greater muscle strength symmetry at all follow-ups but lower absolute strength normalized to bodyweight in the uninjured limb, except hamstrings strength at 10 weeks. Patients in the rehabilitation group reported higher KOOS symptoms at 8- and 12 months and sports/recreation at 10 weeks, present K-SES18 was higher at 10 weeks but lower at 12 months, while future K-SES18 was lower at all follow-ups. Patients in the rehabilitation alone group reported lower ACL-RSI was lower at 12 months and Tegner activity levels were lower pre-injury and at all follow-ups.
CONCLUSIONS: Patients treated with rehabilitation alone had greater symmetrical strength, but lower uninjured limb absolute strength normalized to bodyweight compared to patients treated with ACLR. Patients in the rehabilitation alone group also reported less knee symptoms, but inferior present and future knee self-efficacy compared with patients treated with ACLR.

title: Effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation applied simultaneously with exercise therapy in patellofemoral pain: A single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simultaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) during exercise may augment task-specific quadriceps activation, but its additional effects in patellofemoral pain (PFP) are uncertain. This pilot trial examined whether adding simultaneous NMES improved pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, quadriceps strength, and muscle thickness compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation.
METHODS: In this single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled pilot trial, 30 participants were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group or acontrol group. Both groups received the same hip- and knee-targeted exercise therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks. The intervention group received NMES during leg press and leg extension exercises, whereas the control group wore the same device with stimulation intensity set to zero. The primary outcome was worst pain during the previous week, assessed using the visual analogue scale(VAS). Secondary outcomes included the anterior knee pain scale (AKPS), Y-Balance Test (YBT) composite score, isokinetic quadriceps strength (60°/s, 180°/s), and quadriceps muscle thickness.
RESULTS: No additional between-group benefit was detected for worst pain (p = .96; Cohen's d = -0.03), AKPS (p = .26; Cohen's d = -0.24), YBT composite (p = .28; Cohen's d = -0.26), isokinetic strength at 60°/s (p = .67; Cohen's d = -0.11), or 180°/s (p = .56; Cohen's d = -0.12). Total quadriceps muscle thickness increased more in the intervention group than in the control group, but the effect was small (p = .03; Cohen's d = -0.27). No adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: No additional short-term benefit of adding simultaneous NMES to exercise therapy was detected for pain, knee-related function, dynamic stability, or quadriceps strength compared with exercise therapy plus sham stimulation. A small increase in total quadriceps muscle thickness was detected, but its clinical relevance remains uncertain. These findings do not support routine addition of simultaneous NMES for short-term pain relief or functional improvement.

title: Interatrial Septal Disorders are Independently Associated with Delayed Post-Exercise Heart Rate Recovery in Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interatrial septal disorders (IASD) are among the most common congenital cardiac anomalies. Their impact on cardiac autonomic function in athletes remains poorly defined. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the prevalence of IASD and their association with cardiac autonomic function, assessed by heart rate recovery (HRR), in a cohort of adult athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study enrolled 1,018 adult athletes undergoing pre-participation cardiovascular screening at the Exercise and Sports Medicine Unit of ''A. Cardarelli'' Hospital, Campobasso, Italy, between January 2024 and May 2025. Trans-thoracic echocardiography with contrast imaging was performed to diagnose IASD. HRR was assessed during exercise stress testing using the Modified Bruce Protocol. ΔHRR was calculated as the change from peak heart rate during exercise to that measured during 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th minutes of recovery.
RESULTS: IASD were identified in 331 athletes (32.5%), including patent foramen ovale (12.5%), redundant interatrial septum (21.7%), atrial septal aneurysm (3.3%), and ostium secundum (1.7%). Athletes with IASD exhibited significantly lower ΔHRR at 1 min (30.8 ± 13.9 vs. 39.9 ± 18.1 bpm, p < 0.001) and 2 min (61.0 ± 17.9 vs. 66.1 ± 16.7 bpm, p < 0.001) post-exercise. On multivariable regression, IASD was the strongest independent predictor of impaired ΔHRR 1 (β =- 11.19, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: IASD are prevalent in athletes and independently associated with delayed post-exercise early HRR, suggesting an impairment in post-exercise vagal reactivation.

title: Running Gait Biomechanics Associated With Tibial Bone Stress Injuries Among Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tibial bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among adolescent runners; however, no studies have evaluated running biomechanics associated with tibial BSI in adolescents.
OBJECTIVE: To describe biomechanical and clinical features among adolescents with a history of tibial BSI, and compare with healthy age- and sex-matched controls.
DESIGN: Retrospective cross-sectional case-control study.
SETTING: Large tertiary-care hospital and affiliated sports injury prevention center.
PARTICIPANTS: Sixty-six adolescents with history of tibial BSI (16.2 ± 1.8 years, BMI: 21.4 ± 3.0 kg/m2) were compared with 66 age- and sex-matched adolescents without a history of tibial BSI (16.3 ± 1.9 years, BMI: 21.7 ± 2.6 kg/m2).
INTERVENTIONS: Medical record review was conducted for tibia BSI case participants. Data from gait analyses completed on an instrumented treadmill.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Participant demographics were compared using independent samples t-tests. Continuous outcome measures [stride length, cadence, %stance phase, and peak mass-normalized vertical ground reaction force (vGRF)], and vertical average load rates (VALR), were compared between groups using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, with Cohen d effect sizes reported.
RESULTS: Study participants with history of tibial BSI demonstrated increased VALR (μ = 1141, P = 0.01, d = 0.29), increased mass-normalized maximum vGRF (μ = 1657, P = 0.02, d = 0.24), and greater % stance phase (μ = 1392, P < 0.001, d = 0.36).
CONCLUSION: Adolescents with a history of tibial BSI demonstrated characteristic gait biomechanics including greater VALR, greater mass-normalized maximum vGRF, and more terrestrial gait pattern. These features should be considered in management of adolescent tibial BSI.

title: Smartphone Accelerometer Assessment of HRV: Concurrent Agreement of the KubiosHRV App.
abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) is widely used to monitor athlete recovery and adaptation. Recent technological advances have enabled HRV assessment through smartphone applications without the need for external devices. This study aimed to assess the concurrent agreement between the accelerometer-based HRV measurement feature of the KubiosHRV app and the Polar H10 in supine, seated, and standing positions. A total of 52 participants (30 males and 22 females) across performance tiers 0-4 completed a 2 min resting recording, with the first minute discarded and the second minute analysed in each position. HRV was measured simultaneously using a Polar H10 chest strap and the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app on an iPhone 14. The analysed variables included Mean RR, RMSSD, SDNN, LF power, HF power, SD1, and SD2. Data were automatically processed by the KubiosHRV app and manually extracted into a database. Results showed excellent intraclass correlation coefficients (≥0.985) and small magnitudes of error for time-domains and non-linear variables in the three analysed positions with the reference criterion. Frequency-domain variables showed larger error estimates. Bland-Altman analysis showed no evidence of proportional bias across the measurement range (p > 0.05). These findings suggest that, during 1 min recordings, the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app showed strong concurrent agreement with the Polar H10 for time-domain variables and acceptable agreement for selected non-linear variables across positions. Therefore, it may represent a practical alternative for routine monitoring of these HRV metrics when external hardware is unavailable.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.
