title: Effects of caffeine supplementation on exercise-induced muscle damage: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) commonly occurs following unaccustomed or high-intensity exercise and is characterized by delayed-onset muscle soreness, elevated muscle damage biomarkers, and transient declines in muscle function. Caffeine, a widely consumed ergogenic aid, has been proposed to mitigate these adverse effects; however, the evidence across studies remains equivocal. This systematic review aimed to synthesize findings from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the effects of caffeine supplementation on markers of EIMD.
METHODS: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by citation tracking. RCTs published between 2005 and 2025 that included human participants and reported direct or indirect indicators of EIMD were eligible. Fifteen RCTs (n = 222) were included and assessed for methodological quality using the PEDro scale.
RESULTS: Caffeine doses ranged from 3 to 6 mg/kg. Among the 6 studies assessing delayed-onset muscle soreness, 4 reported significant reductions in perceived soreness within 24 to 48 hours post-exercise, whereas 2 found no effect or adverse responses. Eleven studies examined biochemical markers; most detected no significant differences between caffeine and placebo, while 2 observed higher creatine kinase levels in the caffeine group. Five studies evaluated functional performance; some indicated attenuation of decrements in maximal voluntary isometric contraction or isokinetic torque, although results were inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: Caffeine supplementation may transiently reduce subjective muscle soreness and, under certain conditions, help preserve muscle function following EIMD, but its effects on biochemical markers are inconsistent. The overall efficacy appears to depend on factors such as exercise modality, dosage, timing, and inter-individual variability. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized protocols are needed to clarify caffeine's role in muscle damage and recovery.

title: Prospective Polynomial Characterization of Tibial Plateau Geometry Shows No Association With Contralateral ACL Injury in Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are common in athletic people, with young female athletes at particularly high risk. After ACL injury, reconstruction, and return to sport, many sustain contralateral ACL (CACL) injuries. While tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry has been associated with first-time ACL injury risk, its role in subsequent CACL injury remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: The normal knee of female athletes who suffered a first-time ACL injury, underwent reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and subsequently suffered a CACL injury will have tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry that is different compared with an equivalent population who did not sustain a subsequent CACL injury.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: A total of 199 subjects who suffered a first-time ACL injury, had reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and had a contralateral knee that was normal underwent bilateral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan acquisitions. Tibial plateau cartilage geometry was assessed on the uninjured, normal knees using T1-weighted Fast Field Echo MRI. Parasagittal slices at maximum cartilage concavity in medial and lateral compartments of the tibia were characterized by fitting fifth-order polynomials. Female athletes who sustained a CACL injury within 4 years of reconstruction and return to sport (n = 12) were matched and compared with a group of female athletes who did not sustain CACL injury (n = 24). Random coefficient mixed-effects regression was used to assess group differences in polynomial functions.
RESULTS: No significant differences in tibial cartilage surface geometry were found between the first-time ACL and first-time ACL + CACL injury groups in the medial (P = 0.23) and lateral (P = 0.18) compartments.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that characterization of tibial plateau cartilage geometry in the normal knee of subjects who underwent reconstruction after a first-time ACL injury is insufficient to predict who will on go on to suffer a subsequent CACL injury.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: More comprehensive predictive models incorporating anatomic, biomechanical, and psychological factors are likely needed to identify those at increased risk for CACL injury after a first-time ACL injury and reconstruction.

title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) causes pain and functional limitation. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is increasingly used as a supportive treatment. Optimal rehabilitation after PRP is unclear. This study investigated the effectiveness of a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach on pain and function.
METHODS: Sixty participants with SAPS were randomized to two groups; 54 completed the study and were included in the final per-protocol analysis (27 per group). During a 21-day period, the study group received a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach in addition to standard conventional physiotherapy, while the control group received standard conventional physiotherapy alone. Range of motion, muscle strength, and posture were evaluated. In addition, outcome measures included the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), Functional Impairment Test-Hand and Neck/Shoulder/Arm (FIT-HaNSA) and Constant-Murley Shoulder Score, which were administered for assessment purposes.
RESULTS: Corbin Posture Scale scores decreased in both groups (p < 0.05). Pain reduction was greater in the study group (VAS: from 9.00 ± 0.67 to 2.92 ± 1.14 versus from 9.11 ± 0.64 to 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: from 27.07 ± 4.41 to 10.07 ± 3.33 versus from 21.33 ± 2.46 to 19.37 ± 2.35; p < 0.001). Improvements in Constant-Murley, DASH, and FIT-HaNSA scores, shoulder muscle strength, and active and passive range of motion were significantly greater in the study group (p < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to standard conventional physiotherapy may provide additional short-term improvements in pain, muscle strength, range of motion, and shoulder function compared with standard conventional physiotherapy alone in individuals with SAPS. However, long-term follow-up was not conducted. Therefore, the sustainability of the observed improvements remains unclear. Future studies should investigate the long-term effects of structured post-PRP rehabilitation approaches.

title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.
METHODS: In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.
RESULTS: EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: -10.9%, 95%CI: -21.4;-0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: -9.80, 95%CI: -18.3;-1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.
CONCLUSION: n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes.
METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate).
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.

title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection.
PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study.
METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales.
RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.
journal: Journal of hand therapy : official journal of the American Society of Hand Therapists

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.
journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine

title: Assessment of Pain and Functional Recovery Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Combined With Secretome Injection.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Predictable graft healing following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction remains a clinical challenge, particularly because insufficient ligamentization and tendon-bone integration may be associated with graft failure and less favorable functional outcomes. Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretome represents a cell-free biological approach comprising diverse bioactive molecules with potential regenerative properties, as supported by preclinical studies. This study aimed to compare pain intensity and functional outcomes at six months after ACL reconstruction using a peroneus longus tendon (PLT) autograft, with and without adjunctive intralesional administration of MSC-derived secretome.
METHODS: This study enrolled 24 patients undergoing arthroscopic single-bundle anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using a peroneus longus tendon (PLT) autograft. Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive either an intralesional injection of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretome into the graft (secretome group, n = 12) or an equivalent-volume saline placebo (control group, n = 12). Clinical outcomes were assessed preoperatively and at 6 months postoperatively using the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) Subjective Knee Evaluation Form, Tegner-Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale, and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain intensity. Between-group comparisons were conducted using the independent-samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, and followed by ANCOVA analysis as appropriate to the distributional characteristics of the data. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: At baseline, IKDC and VAS scores did not differ significantly between the secretome and control groups (IKDC: 48.57 ± 4.91 vs. 47.51 ± 4.45, p > 0.05; VAS: 7.75 ± 0.62 in both groups, p = 1.000). At the six months follow-up, patients receiving adjunctive secretome injection demonstrated significantly higher IKDC scores than controls (86.89 ± 5.11 vs. 78.27 ± 3.91, p < 0.01). Similarly, Tegner-Lysholm scores were significantly higher in the secretome group (87.08 ± 5.16 vs. 79.33 ± 2.67, p < 0.01). Pain intensity was also significantly lower in the secretome group, as reflected by lower VAS scores (2.17 ± 0.72 vs. 3.92 ± 0.79, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Adjunctive MSC-derived secretome administration during anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using a peroneus longus tendon (PLT) autograft was associated with higher International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective knee scores and Tegner-Lysholm knee scores, as well as lower Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores, at 6 months postoperatively compared with saline placebo. These findings suggest the potential of MSC-derived secretome as a cell-free biological adjunct to improve patient-reported knee function and reduce postoperative pain following ACL reconstruction, warranting further evaluation in larger clinical trials.

title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study examined how hamstring muscle-tendon unit length influences critical torque (CT), work capacity above CT (W'), and the mechanisms of motor performance fatigue during and after repeated maximal voluntary contractions.
METHODS: Twelve healthy men (25 ± 4 years) performed, on separate days, two fatiguing protocols consisting of fifty 3-s maximal isometric knee flexions (2-s rest) at joint-angle configurations expected to produce relatively long (LL) and short (SL) hamstring muscle-tendon unit lengths. Neuromuscular assessments were conducted before, during, and up to 15 min post-exercise. CT and W' were determined from the torque-duration relationship. Peripheral fatigue was evaluated using peak evoked torques (T100), and central fatigue using voluntary activation (VA) derived from the twitch interpolation technique. Linear mixed-effects models and paired t-tests assessed the effects of time and joint-angle configuration.
RESULTS: CT did not differ between LL and SL (p = 0.65), whereas W' was significantly lower at SL than LL (p < 0.001, d = 0.96). MVC torque decreased by ~45% after fatiguing protocols (p < 0.001, η 2p = 0.84), accompanied by reductions in T100 (-22%) and VA (-17). During recovery, VA returned to baseline within 3 min, while T100 remained depressed throughout recovery (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In the knee flexors, short muscle-tendon unit length reduces the capacity to perform work above CT without altering CT or the magnitude and etiology of fatigue. The rapid recovery of voluntary activation alongside persistent peripheral impairment extends current knowledge of recovery kinetics specifically for repeated maximal knee-flexion exercise.
journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

title: Time-Efficient Reactive Agility Training Improves Motor and Cognitive Components of Reactive Agility in Open- and Closed-Skill Athletes: A 6-Week Intervention Study.
abstract: Reactive agility (RA), the ability to respond to external stimuli with whole-body movements as quickly and precisely as possible, is crucial for many sports, particularly open-skill sports, and is influenced by both motor and cognitive abilities. This study aims to investigate which of the underlying components of RA is most improved through RA training, whether prior experience with RA movements influences the rate of improvement, and whether a time-ecological approach also leads to improvements. Assessments included 19 open-skill and 26 closed-skill athletes with different competitive backgrounds. RA training was carried out once a week for six weeks with each session lasting 20 minutes. Pre- and post-assessments were conducted for RA (Random Star Run), change-of-direction (t-Test), and cognitive performance (Stroop test). Baseline differences between open- and closed-skill athletes and performance level were evaluated using 2 × 2 ANOVA. Intervention effects were calculated using repeated measures ANOVA. Open-skill athletes were significantly faster within the RA task than closed-skill athletes (p = 0.017; F = 6.247; η2 p = 0.132). Both groups improved significantly across all outcome measures (p < 0.05; RA and both underlying properties) with no interaction effects of group × time (p > 0.05). One weekly 20-min training session is sufficient to improve RA, and selected motor and cognitive performance parameters. Prior experience, based on regular participation in open-skill sports, seems to be associated with higher RA performance but does not moderate training adaptations, as both groups improved similarly in RA and the underlying motor and cognitive functions.

title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
abstract: Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

title: Tired of Thinking? Think Again! A Longitudinal Experience-Sampling Study of Bidirectional Dynamics Between Rumination and Mental Fatigue in Athletes.
abstract: Recovery days are intended to support psychological and physical recovery, yet repetitive sport-related thinking may interfere with this process. This four-week experience-sampling study examined the dynamic interplay between rumination and mental fatigue during rest days in competitive athletes, as well as the moderating roles of perfectionistic concerns and perfectionistic strivings. A total of 134 athletes completed repeated rest-day assessments of rumination and mental fatigue, with perfectionism measured at baseline using a sport-adapted version of the FMPS-Brief. Continuous-time structural equation modelling revealed significant bidirectional coupling between rumination and mental fatigue, supporting a self-reinforcing dynamic in which rumination fuels fatigue, and accumulated fatigue heightens the likelihood of further rumination, creating a 'vicious cycle'. The rumination → mental fatigue pathway was stronger than the reverse, underscoring the critical importance of mental rest and psychological recovery in sport. Perfectionistic concerns significantly moderated this association, suggesting that athletes high in evaluative self-criticism may be more vulnerable to the rumination-fatigue cycle, whereas perfectionistic strivings did not exert a moderating effect. These findings advance a process-oriented understanding of psychological recovery in athletes and may inform future research on how short-term rumination-fatigue dynamics contribute to longer-term maladaptive recovery patterns, including burnout risk. Interventions targeting repetitive negative thinking, such as mindfulness-, cognitive-behavioral-, or acceptance-based approaches, may help athletes preserve psychological recovery under performance demands.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: More than a shot: function over pain with tele-supervised resistance exercise added to hyaluronic acid injection in knee osteoarthritis, a randomized add-on trial.
abstract: Exercise is central to knee osteoarthritis (KOA) care, and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (IAHA) is often used as an adjunct, yet access to supervised exercise after injection is limited. Whether adding tele-supervised resistance band exercise (TSBE) improves outcomes beyond IAHA alone is unclear. Eighty adults with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 1-3 KOA who had not responded adequately to conservative care received a single IAHA injection and were allocated to a 12-week TSBE or standard education without supervised exercise. The between-group difference in Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total change favoured TSBE (-5 points, 95% CI - 9.86 to -0.13; p = .044). TSBE also favoured WOMAC physical function (-4.88, 95% CI - 8.28 to -1.47), 30-second sit-to-stand (+3.79 repetitions, 95% CI 2.80 to 4.79), and timed up-and-go (-1.87 s, 95% CI - 2.34 to -1.41), but not VAS pain (-0.38, 95% CI - 1.00 to 0.25). Adding TSBE to IAHA improved function and mobility, with no additional reduction in pain.

title: Adjustment of the Anteroposterior Center-of-Pressure Position Reduces Asymmetrical Knee Loading During Double-Leg Squatting After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract: Asymmetrical knee extension moments (KEMs) are associated with poor clinical outcomes following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. However, effective corrective methods remain limited. Thirty-four individuals (144.1 [60.2] d postanterior cruciate ligament reconstruction) performed 12 sets of 5 squats with visual feedback to maintain a symmetrical anteroposterior center-of-pressure position. Limb symmetry indices were calculated for KEM, vertical ground reaction force, and knee-to-support moment ratio (knee moment divided by the sum of hip, knee, and ankle extension moments). A mixed-model analysis of variance examined the effects of group (asymmetry: baseline KEM limb symmetry indices < 90%; symmetry: ≥90%) and time (baseline, post-biofeedback). Biomechanical changes were observed primarily within the asymmetry group (21 participants), which showed increases in limb symmetry indices for KEM (73.0% [10.5%] vs 85.4% [15.5%], P < .001), knee-to-support moment ratio (81.0% [16.7%] vs 87.4% [14.8%], P = .006), and vertical ground reaction force (90.5% [7.1%] vs 96.3% [8.6%], P = .003). Notably, these differences were primarily driven by changes in the uninvolved limb rather than the involved limb. No significant changes were observed in the symmetry group. While biofeedback of the anteroposterior center-of-pressure position reduced asymmetrical knee loading, further strategies are required to specifically elicit changes in the involved limb.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: Immediate Return or Overnight Stay? Sleep Responses by Postmatch Travel Strategy and Match Participation in Professional Football.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Late European away fixtures can disrupt sleep, but the influence of immediate return versus overnight stay, and whether responses differ by match participation, remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: Postmatch travel strategy would influence sleep quality and duration across the prematch, match, and subsequent nights, with responses moderated by match participation.
STUDY DESIGN: Observational repeated-measures field study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: A total of 19 outfield English Premier League players were monitored across 10 European away fixtures (5 immediate return and 5 overnight stay). Self-reported sleep quality (1 to 7) and sleep duration were recorded on the prematch, match, and subsequent nights. Fixed-effects models examined condition, time, and match participation, with standard errors clustered by player.
RESULTS: Sleep quality was lower than prematch baseline on the match and subsequent nights (both β = -0.62 arbitrary units [AU]; P < 0.01; g = -0.63). After overnight stay, sleep quality improved from the match to the subsequent night in players who participated and those who did not (β = 0.69 and 0.63 AU; 95% CIs, 0.37-0.90 and 0.47-0.91; P < 0.01), whereas no change occurred after immediate return. Across participation groups, sleep duration was lower after overnight stay than immediate return on the match night (β = -1.94 hours; P < 0.01; g = -1.26) and subsequent night (β = -1.02 hours; P = 0.02; g = -0.67). However, after overnight stay, sleep duration increased between these nights by 1.45 hours in participants and 1.43 hours in nonparticipants (P < 0.01), with no significant change after immediate return. Participation moderated sleep duration on both postfixture nights (β = 1.27 and 1.64 hours; P ≤ 0.04; g = 0.82 and 1.07).
CONCLUSION: Neither travel strategy was uniformly superior. Overnight stay was associated with poorer absolute sleep duration but a clearer next-night rebound in sleep quality and duration.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Postmatch travel should be planned case by case, considering itinerary, next-day demands, and individual match exposure rather than applying a single team-wide policy.

title: A two-factor framework to assess international male field hockey movement characteristics: Implications for performance preparation.
abstract: We aimed to establish the nature and structure of the relationships between high-intensity movement characteristics during international field hockey matches. Global positioning system data were obtained from 28 elite male field hockey players (n = 393 international player-matches). Mean and 90% trimmed range were extracted for the 10 most intense 1-min periods (separated by >60s) for: total distance (m); high-speed distance (>5 m·s-1); sprint distance (>7 m·s-1); accelerations (>2.5 m·s-2); decelerations (<-2.5 m·s-2) and high-speed cuts (>45° change-of-direction at >5 m·s-1). Pearson's correlations were calculated for pairs of characteristics (summed across the 10 most intense periods). An exploratory factor analysis was then applied to movement characteristics. Finally, factors were validated by testing whether they discriminated between playing positions using random-effect linear-mixed models. Factor analysis explained 76% of total variance (χ42 = 286, p < 0.001) and resulted in a two-factor solution: 'Distance' (total, high-speed and sprint distance), and 'Acceleration' (accelerations and decelerations). High-speed cuts loaded onto both factors. The two factors also discriminated significantly between playing positions. Our data-driven approach indicates that Distance and Acceleration are distinct factors of international male field hockey, specifically, Midfielders cover more distance than Defenders, and Strikers change speed and direction more than Midfielders or Defenders. Practitioners should consider prescribing and monitoring these distinct factors separately.

title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

title: Supervised Combined Exercise as an Intervention in Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Mixed-Methods Case Report.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) remains a severe clinical condition associated with persistent symptomatology, functional impairment, and unhealthy lifestyle patterns. This case report examines the effects of a supervised combined exercise intervention using a mixed-methods approach. A 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of TRD treated with clomipramine (150 mg/day), lamotrigine (400 mg/day), and bromazepam (3 mg/day) presented with moderate depressive symptoms (Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale [MADRS] = 28; Clinical Global Impressions Scale [CGI-S] = 4), marked sedentary behavior (approximately 13 h/day), low cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) (VO2peak = 18 mL·kg-1·min-1), and elevated fat mass (42%). She participated in a 12-week supervised combined exercise programme (aerobic and resistance training, twice weekly) within the TRACE-RMD framework. Following the intervention, depressive symptoms decreased by 57% (MADRS = 12), with remission of global illness severity (CGI-S = 1) and a 16.7% increase in CRF. Functional disability and perceived stress were substantially reduced, while perceived social support markedly increased, as assessed by the Sheehan Disability Inventory (the global score reflects disability, item 4 reflects perceived stress, and item 5 reflects social support). Qualitative narratives indicated improvements in mood regulation, reduced rumination, increased self-efficacy, and enhanced social reintegration. Supervised combined exercise may represent a feasible and clinically meaningful adjunctive intervention in TRD, acting not only on symptom reduction but also on functional recovery and psychosocial re-engagement. Further controlled studies are warranted.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov identifier (NCT05136027).

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

title: Multi-planar patellar hypomobility as a potential contributor to VMO-VL dyssynergy and return to sport limitations following ACL reconstruction in soccer players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patellofemoral hypomobility (PFH) is a frequent yet underestimated complication following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. PFH induces biomechanical and neuromuscular alterations that impair return to sport (RTS) and accelerate early joint degeneration. However, current evidence describes PFH primarily as an associated factor rather than a direct causal determinant of RTS failure. Therefore, the primary objective of this review is to analyze the correlation between PFH and functional complications during RTS. The study also aims to summarize the available evidence on the relationship between PFH and medium- to long-term clinical outcomes, without implying causal predictions where not supported.
METHODS: A narrative review was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science using a Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO)-structured search. No systematic review procedures or pooled quantitative analyses were performed; all numerical data derived from individual studies. Included studies involved athletes aged 18-35 undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BPTB) or Hamstring autografts.
RESULTS: The analysis reveals significant PFH (>25% compared to the contralateral side) in 15-22% of athletes at 6 months, with a peak of 28% in BPTB graft cases. Longitudinal hypomobility correlates with extension deficit, whereas transverse hypomobility is associated with increased anterior knee pain (AKP) in 34% of cases. Data indicate a 12-15% reduction in Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance and a 3.4-fold higher risk of patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) within 5 years, although PFH was not directly measured as an independent variable in these studies. Additionally, 25% of athletes with PFH discontinue competitive activity within 36 months after RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: PFH emerges as an important factor associated with postoperative functional limitations. Restricted patellar glide disrupts the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)/vastus lateralis (VL) synergy, reduces performance, and accelerates cartilage degeneration. Symmetry of patellar kinematics should be considered a relevant parameter for RTS decision-making, while acknowledging that RTS outcomes are multifactorial and not solely determined by PFH.

title: Earlier and More Criteria-Based Return to Sport After Pediatric Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in North America Compared With the Asia-Pacific Region: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the management and rehabilitation strategies for pediatric anterior cruciate ligament injuries between North America and the Asia-Pacific region.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library was performed for studies published between January 2020 and August 2025. Articles were included if they described pediatric anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation protocols for patients 18 years and younger. Included studies consisted primarily of retrospective studies, cohort studies, case series, technical notes, and cross-sectional studies (Levels II-IV). Data were extracted on bracing use and duration, weight-bearing status, range-of-motion restrictions, sports progression, and return-to-sport criteria.
RESULTS: Forty studies were included (27 North America, 13 Asia-Pacific). Bracing was used frequently in both North America (86%) and Asia-Pacific (72%), with North American protocols often specifying duration (2-6 weeks) or criteria-based discontinuation, whereas Asia-Pacific protocols frequently omitted details. Early range-of-motion restoration was advocated in both regions (North America 85%, Asia-Pacific 91%), although restrictions were applied when meniscal repair was performed. Both regions supported early weight-bearing regardless of surgical technique. Both regions shared similar timelines for running and jogging restrictions; however, North American centers (60%) introduced sport-specific drills earlier between 3 and 6 months. Return-to-sport clearance was delayed beyond 9 months in most protocols (North America 46%, Asia-Pacific 62%). North American center, however, showed more flexibility with 46% allowing return-to-sport clearance before 9 months. North American centers more often incorporated functional criteria (50%) alongside time-based measures, whereas Asia-Pacific centers relied primarily on time-based thresholds.
CONCLUSIONS: Early rehabilitation protocols after pediatric anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction were similar between North America and the Asia-Pacific region with respect to bracing, weight-bearing, and range-of-motion practices. However, return-to-sport progression differed because North American centers more frequently introduced sport-specific activities earlier and more commonly incorporated functional criteria in addition to time-based thresholds, whereas Asia-Pacific centers more often relied on time-based clearance and delayed sport-specific progression.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV evidence.

title: Musculoskeletal injury epidemiology among football players in Africa: A systematic review of injury incidence, patterns and associated factors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Football is widely played across Africa, yet evidence on the epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries among African football players remains fragmented across countries, populations, and competitive settings. Differences in injury definitions, surveillance methods, and exposure measurement further limit comparison between studies. This systematic review synthesised the available evidence on musculoskeletal injury epidemiology in African football.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database, and Google Scholar were systematically searched from inception to the final search date, supplemented by backward citation searching. Studies investigating musculoskeletal injuries among football players in Africa were eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Methodological quality and risk of bias were evaluated using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tools, as appropriate. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-six studies were included. Sixteen studies contributed 18 incidence estimates, ranging from 2.2 to 289 injuries per 1,000 athlete-exposure hours, while 10 studies reported prevalence estimates ranging from 4.1% to 81.6%. Tournament surveillance studies generally reported higher incidence than season-long studies, and match incidence exceeded training incidence where both were reported. Lower-extremity injuries predominated, particularly at the ankle and knee, while sprains or ligament injuries, contusions, and muscle-related injuries were the most frequently reported injury types. Previous injury or recurrence was the most consistently identified associated factor.
CONCLUSION: Musculoskeletal injuries are common in African football, but substantial methodological heterogeneity limits direct comparison of estimates. Standardised injury surveillance and stronger prospective research are needed to improve the evidence base and support context-specific injury prevention.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Anthocyanin-Rich Aronia melanocarpa Supplementation Modulates Intestinal Barrier Biomarkers and Stress-Axis Response in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anthocyanin-rich berries may modulate intestinal barrier-related processes and physiological stress responses, but evidence from human studies remains limited.
METHODS: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 15 elite male rowers (Aronia group, n = 7; placebo group, n = 8). Participants received Aronia melanocarpa supplementation or placebo for eight weeks and performed a standardized 2000-m rowing ergometer test before and after the intervention. Circulating claudin-3 (CLDN-3), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP), and cortisol concentrations were assessed before exercise, immediately after exercise, and following 1 h of recovery.
RESULTS: A significant Group × Time interaction was observed for CLDN-3 (p = 0.0463). After eight weeks, pre-exercise CLDN-3 concentrations were lower in the Aronia group than in the placebo group (p = 0.0367). Lower pre-exercise LBP concentrations (p = 0.0125) and lower cortisol concentrations at 1 h post-exercise (p = 0.0079) were also observed in the Aronia group compared with placebo. No significant supplementation-specific effect was observed for I-FABP.
CONCLUSIONS: Eight weeks of Aronia melanocarpa supplementation was associated with differences in selected intestinal barrier-related biomarkers and post-exercise cortisol concentrations in elite male rowers. However, these findings were primarily related to specific sampling time points and should not be interpreted as evidence of improved intestinal barrier function. Given the small sample size and potential dietary confounding, the results are preliminary and require confirmation in larger randomized controlled trials.

title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.
METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.
RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.
CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort.
METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score).
RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed.
DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation and exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis: A mixed-methods pilot randomised controlled trial.
abstract: This mixed-methods pilot trial evaluated the feasibility and patient perceptions of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. Twenty-four participants were allocated to active or sham home-based tDCS plus exercise. Participants completed 10 tDCS sessions over two weeks and an eight-week exercise program, with laboratory assessments at baseline, week four, and week eight. Primary outcomes were recruitment, adherence, adverse events, attrition, and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included local pressure pain thresholds, pain, function, quality of life, and semi-structured interviews exploring intervention facilitators and barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data using inductive thematic analysis. All prespecified feasibility and safety criteria were met. Adherence was high, with 88% of participants (21/24) completing at least 75% of tDCS sessions, and 75% (18/24) completing at least 75% of exercise sessions. No significant adverse events occurred. Mean (SD) pain intensity /100 decreased from 47.3 (25.6) to 28.3 (16.1) in the active group and from 46.4 (17.8) to 33.5 (16.7) in the sham group at week 8. A future trial would require 80 participants. Qualitative themes indicated that evidence of effectiveness was more important to engagement than financial cost, tDCS was viewed as an appealing alternative to pharmacological treatment, and initial device operation was a greater barrier than safety or home use. Home-based tDCS combined with exercise was feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable intervention improves pain and function in people with knee osteoarthritis. PERSPECTIVE: This pilot trial indicates that home-based tDCS combined with exercise is feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated for knee osteoarthritis. Participants valued its convenience and non-pharmacological nature. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable approach improves pain and function and broadens access to care.

title: Return to Sport and Clinical Outcomes after Surgical Stabilization of Chronic Ankle Instability in Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) can compromise athletic performance and delay return to competition. Although primary ligament repair and ligament reconstruction are valid surgical options, comparative data remains limited.
PURPOSE: The primary aim was to evaluate overall return-to-sport outcomes after surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability in athletes. The secondary aim was to compare return-to-sport and postoperative clinical outcomes between direct ligament repair and ligament reconstruction.
STUDY DESIGN: Comparative retrospective study METHODS: This comparative cohort study included 54 athletes who underwent surgical stabilization for CAI between 2018 and 2024. Surgical procedures were categorized as primary repair and ligament reconstruction. The primary outcomes were RTS status and time to RTS. Secondary outcomes included postoperative Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) scores and residual complaints.
RESULTS: The mean age was 25.6 ± 6.9 years, and 48% of patients were football players. The median interval from the latest injury to surgery was 6.0 months. RTS status was available for 49 of the 54 athletes (91%). Of these, 48 (98%) returned to sport at a mean time of 5.3 months (range 2.0 to 16.0), while one athlete did not return to sport. Postoperative functional outcomes were favorable, with mean FAAM activities of daily living and sport scores of 96.2 ± 8.3 and 89.7 ± 20.4, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed among surgical groups in RTS status, time to RTS, FAAM scores, or residual complaints.
CONCLUSION: Surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability was associated with favorable postoperative scores and a high RTS rate among athletes with available outcome data. The sample size and overall study design preclude conclusions regarding the equivalence or superiority of repair versus reconstruction.

title: Updates on Low Energy Availability in Athletes: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and the Female or Male Athlete Triad.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This paper evaluates the latest literature on low energy availability (LEA) in athletes, which is the basis for the clinical conditions known as the Female Athlete Triad, Male Athlete Triad, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). It explores how these different conditions are related, and how the clinician can approach screening, diagnosis, and management of LEA in athletes.
RECENT FINDINGS: Within the past five years the Male Athlete Triad Consensus Statements were published in 2021, expanding upon knowledge regarding LEA in the Female Athlete Triad and applying this to the male population. Additionally, there has been an important update to the REDs model and a new clinical assessment tool (CAT2) published in 2023. This is based on new research into the different physiologic and psychologic sequelae of LEA. This has sparked additional discussion regarding the diagnosis, management, and prevention of LEA. The consequences of LEA can be severe, and can affect multiple different organ systems. Treatment should ideally involve a multidisciplinary team consisting of a physician, dietitian, and mental health provider, but may also include additional professionals such as athletic trainers, physical therapists, physiologists, other medical specialists, or other members of the athlete support system (including family and coaches). The mainstay of management remains optimizing energy availability (EA) through improving macro and micronutrient intake, and also requires addressing some of the more common sequelae of LEA. Prevention largely focuses on educational efforts and fostering healthy environments, particularly when discussing weight, body composition, and performance.
