title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: [Research progress on correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament injury and bone bruise].
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To review the research progress on the correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and bone bruise.
METHODS: Relevant literature on non-contact ACL injury and bone bruise published in recent years was reviewed. The imaging characteristics and injury mechanisms of bone bruise, factors affecting bone bruise distribution, the associations between bone bruise and combined intra-articular injuries, and the impact of bone bruise on postoperative outcomes after ACL reconstruction were summarized and analyzed.
RESULTS: Bone bruise is a common MRI finding in non-contact ACL injury, mainly involving the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau. The typical "kissing" bone bruise pattern can reflect the abnormal loading condition of the knee joint at the moment of injury and provides important imaging evidence for inferring the injury mechanism of ACL rupture. The occurrence and distribution of bone bruise may be influenced by factors such as age, osseous morphology of the knee, and meniscal anatomical characteristics. The extent, location, and severity of bone bruise are associated with knee laxity, anterolateral ligament injury, meniscal tears, and articular cartilage injury to varying degrees. Among these, the association between lateral compartment bone bruise and lateral meniscal injury is relatively well established, while bone bruise of the medial tibial plateau may indicate occult posterior horn injury of the medial meniscus. Bone bruise may also be associated with early postoperative pain and recovery of knee range of motion after ACL reconstruction, and may increase the risk of cartilage degeneration and post-traumatic osteoarthritis. However, its predictive value for mid- and long-term knee function and clinical outcomes remains inconclusive.
CONCLUSION: Bone bruise can reflect, to some extent, the loading mechanism and severity of non-contact ACL injury, and provides important clues for identifying associated structural injuries and evaluating prognosis. However, the grading and assessment criteria for bone bruise remain unstandardized, and controversies remain regarding its associations with certain combined injuries and long-term clinical outcomes. Further standardized, large-scale, multi-center, and long-term follow-up studies are required to clarify the clinical value of bone bruise in the assessment and prognostic evaluation of ACL injury.

title: Strength Training in Youth: A Scoping Review with Evidence Gap Map.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Strength training has gained increasing attention in youth athletic development due to its benefits in performance and motor competence. However, a comprehensive overview of the literature examining strength training in youth populations is lacking, and research remains fragmented across sex, maturation stages, and intervention characteristics.
OBJECTIVE: To conduct a systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map of studies on strength training in youth aged 6-18 years to provide evidence-based priorities for future research and practice.
METHODS: This scoping review followed PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Studies involving youth athletes exposed to structured strength training interventions (e.g., resistance, bodyweight, or combined methods) were included. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus was conducted up to April 20th, 2025. Data were descriptively summarized using pre-defined themes and tabulation procedures, and an evidence gap map was generated to depict how research is distributed across training variables, outcome domains, and population characteristics.
RESULTS: Out of 3770 records screened, 342 studies were included. Approximately 90% of trials assessed physical performance outcomes (e.g., strength, power, sprint speed), with limited focus on motor competence, injury prevention, or psychosocial factors. Male participants dominated the sample pool, while sex-specific analyses were uncommon. Studies involving biologically mature adolescents were scarce, and intervention durations varied widely, with numerous studies extending beyond eight weeks. A substantial proportion of studies failed to adequately report key training variables, such as frequency, intensity, supervision methods, limiting replicability, and comparability. Strength training was primarily studied in team sport contexts, especially soccer and rugby, with individual sports under-represented. Psychosocial outcomes, contextual factors (e.g., training environment), and follow-up beyond 6 months were absent in most studies. Technological and innovative approaches, including velocity-based and flywheel training, were limited to pilot studies. The evidence gap map revealed critical deficiencies in female representation, long-term follow-up, biological maturation assessment, and multidimensional outcome evaluation.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence indicates that youth strength training has been widely studied in relation to physical performance, injury-related outcomes, and neuromuscular development. However, important evidence gaps remain regarding biological maturity, sex-specific responses, psychosocial outcomes, long-term follow-up and context-specific applications. This scoping review identifies these gaps and highlights key priorities for future research rather than providing definitive recommendations for training practice or policy.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Increased patellar tendon size and stiffness are associated with reduced knee extensor rate of torque development after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with bone-patellar tendon-bone graft.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Knee extensor weakness persists long-term following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) with a bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft, yet the contribution of donor patellar tendon morphology and mechanical properties to these deficits remains unclear. The purpose of this study was to determine whether donor patellar tendon properties were associated with knee extensor rate of torque development (RTD) and peak torque following ACLR with BPTB autograft.
METHODS: Twenty-five individuals (18.4 ± 2.8 years) underwent ultrasonography of the patellar tendon and isometric knee extensor strength testing approximately 3-4.5 months postsurgery. B-mode ultrasound and shear wave elastography were collected bilaterally to assess patellar tendon cross-sectional area (CSA), thickness and regional stiffness.
RESULTS: The donor patellar tendon was significantly larger (p < 0.001), thicker (p < 0.001) and stiffer (p = 0.001) than the uninvolved tendon. Patellar tendon CSA, thickness and stiffness were not associated with peak torque (p = 0.146 to 0.853); however, several properties were identified as negative predictors of RTD. Medial patellar tendon stiffness was the strongest negative predictor of RTD (R 2 = 0.276, p = 0.007), with stiffness, CSA and thickness collectively explaining 40.8% of the variance in RTD (p = 0.010).
CONCLUSIONS: Patellar tendon adaptations after graft harvest were negatively associated with RTD but not peak torque. While not causally established, these findings provide a potential target for rehabilitation aimed at restoring explosive strength after ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Pelvic floor knowledge and unhealthy habits related in female athletes: a cross-sectional study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To describe pelvic floor (PF)-related knowledge and unhealthy habits among female athletes, and to examine their associations with PF dysfunction (PFD) symptoms, sports characteristics, academic level and help seeking attitudes.
METHODS: A total of 538 female athletes (36.7 ± 11.3 years) completed an anonymous online questionnaire covering age, academic level, sports experience, unhealthy PF-related habits, PFD symptoms, professional healthcare-seeking attitude and knowledge about urinary incontinence (UI), anorectal incontinence (ARI), pelvic organ prolapse (POP) and female sexual dysfunction (FSD). Adequate knowledge was considered as ≥70% correct responses.
RESULTS: Female athletes demonstrated adequate knowledge regarding UI, ARI and POP, but insufficient knowledge about FSD (52.6%). Several PFD symptoms were associated with lower knowledge levels and a higher number of unhealthy habits compared with athletes without these symptoms (p<0.05). Younger athletes showed lower knowledge about ARI (p=0.033) and POP (p=0.003), while older athletes showed lower knowledge about FSD (p<0.001). Athletes who rejected professional healthcare showed lower knowledge across all PFD domains (p<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Female athletes reporting symptoms suggestive of PFD showed lower levels of knowledge and a higher number of unhealthy PF habits compared with those without symptoms. Although athletes generally demonstrated an appropriate level of knowledge regarding PFD, important gaps were observed in the FSD domain and in unhealthy toileting and sport-related habits, particularly among athletes without university studies. Differences in knowledge were also observed according to age and healthcare-seeking attitudes, highlighting areas that may be considered in future educational initiatives.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.

title: Case Study Insights Into Female World-Class and Elite Athletes' Training and Physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article offers a structured overview of published case studies involving elite and world-class female Olympic athletes, highlighting the unique insights these studies provide into training characteristics, physiology, performance, and female-specific factors.
METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for peer-reviewed case studies involving tiers 4 to 5 female Olympic athletes reporting individual-level data on training, physiological, and/or performance characteristics.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight studies describing 54 elite and world-class female athletes from 18 countries and 19 Olympic sports met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were published after 2017 (68%), originated from Europe (58%), and involved endurance sports (81%). Fifteen studies examined long-term athlete development, with observation periods ranging from 4 to 26 years. Fourteen studies reported annual training and physiological characteristics across 10 sports including training volume, intensity distribution, periodization, and physiological profiling. Four studies examined altitude training, 8 addressed competition demands, tapering, and precompetition strategies, and 8 focused on female-specific physiology, health, and performance, including energy availability, menstrual function, hormonal cycle monitoring and pregnancy, and postpartum return to sport.
CONCLUSION: Case studies provide unique athlete-centered insights into the complex interactions between training, physiology, health, and performance in elite female athletes. Collectively, they demonstrate that pathways to world-class performance are highly individualized, while generating hypotheses that complement group-based research. Future case studies should prioritize underrepresented sports, geographical regions, and female-specific topics to expand the diversity of performance environments and athlete populations represented in the literature.

title: Effects of Combined Sprint and Plyometric Training vs Plyometric Training only on Physical Fitness and Sport-Specific Performance in Male Pubertal Soccer Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint (ST) and plyometric training (PT) are well-established methods for improving physical fitness and sport-specific performance in youth athletes. However, the effects of their combination remain unclear.
AIM: This study investigated the effects of an 8-week combined ST and PT program (SPT), PT-only program, and active control (CG) on physical fitness and sport-specific performance in young male soccer players.
METHODS: Forty-six pubertal Tier 2 training and performance caliber, male soccer players (13.9-14.2 years; maturity offset = 0.18-0.78 years from peak height velocity) participated in the study. Training was conducted twice weekly (2 × 30 min) over 8 weeks and was integrated into regular soccer sessions. The SPT program consisted of a progressive sequence of plyometric exercises (countermovement, line, drop jumps, and single-leg jumps/push-offs), immediately followed by a prescribed 10-15-m sprint or change-of-direction (CoD) task. The PT group performed the same plyometric exercises and exercise order without the subsequent sprint or CoD component. Training loads were monitored using the OMNI 0-10 RPE scale. The CG continued their regular soccer-specific training. Assessments included dynamic balance, muscle strength (reactive strength) and power (standing long jump, countermovement jump, five-jump test), speed (10-m and 30-m linear sprints), CoD speed with and without the ball, and sport-specific performance (throw-in and standing-kick tests).
RESULTS: Significant group × time interactions were observed for most outcomes (p < 0.05), with partial eta-squared (ηp2) values ranging from 0.33 to 0.81. Significant interactions were found for dynamic balance (ηp2 = 0.66), reactive strength (ηp2 = 0.33), power (ηp2 = 0.65-0.81), 10-m sprint performance (ηp2 = 0.42), CoD speed (ηp2 = 0.44-0.45), and sport-specific performance (ηp2 = 0.73-0.78). Bonferroni-adjusted between-group comparisons indicated significant differences between SPT and PT for selected outcomes, including dynamic balance, power (five-jump and countermovement jump tests), speed (10-m sprint and 15-m CoD without the ball), and throw-in performance, whereas no significant SPT-PT differences were detected for the remaining outcomes. Significant pre-post-improvements were observed across the assessed outcomes in the SPT group, while PT also produced significant improvements in several measures and the CG showed limited or non-significant changes. Although both SPT and PT significantly improved 30-m sprint performance, the group × time interaction did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.060, ηp2 = 0.12).
CONCLUSIONS: An 8-week combined SPT intervention was associated with greater performance than PT alone for selected physical fitness and sport-specific outcomes, particularly dynamic balance, power and throw-in performance, in pubertal male Tier 2 soccer players. However, these benefits were outcome-specific and were not observed across all assessed measures.

title: 3D Biomechanics of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Football: What We Have Learned in the Last Five Years.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most impacting injuries in professional football. Understanding these injuries in their environment, and their biomechanical mechanism, is the bottleneck between injury surveillance and effective mechanism-informed prevention and rehabilitation. We reconstructed the three-dimensional kinematics of 33 cases of ACL injury sustained by elite male football players during official matches. The Model-Based Image-Matching technique was leveraged to obtain quantitative, detailed estimates of three-dimensional joint kinematics, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional bidimensional video analyses. This paper reviews and interprets findings derived from over five years of research on the topic from a novel perspective. At the knee level, ACL injury mechanics involved a sequence of multiplanar joint rotations; on the sagittal plane, knee flexion increased from initial contact to injury frame; on the frontal plane, a knee abduction (valgus) shift emerged; on the transverse plane, following ground contact, we observed a sequence of internal and then external rotation of the femur, relative to the tibia, occurring during loading acceptance. Expanding the analysis on total-body kinematics, marked inter-individual variability was observed across the studied cohort; while ACL failure exhibits consistent kinematic features at the knee level, the sequence of whole-body postures leading to injury appears to be context-dependent. Finally, we propose biomechanically informed approaches to injury mitigation, emphasizing the integration of sport-specific contextual determinants, perceptual and decision-making processes, challenging the traditional separation between technical coaching and injury prevention.

title: Return to sports after pediatric brain tumors: Time to move beyond survival.
abstract: Brain tumors are the second most common malignancy in children and adolescents and the leading cause of cancer-related death in this population. While survival rates have improved, survivors are at risk of neurocognitive, motor, and psychosocial sequelae due to both tumor location and treatments used. Participation in sport is increasingly recognized as beneficial for functional recovery, cardiorespiratory fitness, and overall well-being in children and adolescents treated for brain tumors. However, return to play (RTP) may pose some challenges, particularly in the presence of neurosurgical devices, cranial radiotherapy, or residual neurological deficits. This narrative clinical review summarizes current evidence on the risks of sport-related injuries in pediatric brain tumor patients and survivors, highlighting factors influencing vulnerability, including treatment history and specific sport characteristics. We propose a risk-based framework for RTP evaluation emphasizing individualized coordinated assessment by pediatric oncologists, neurosurgeons, and sports medicine specialists. Protective strategies are discussed, although evidence for concussion prevention remains limited. A safe RTP should be enhanced by the here-proposed structured evaluation, balancing safety with the physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits of active participation. This framework aims to support clinicians and families in facilitating safe and effective reintegration of pediatric brain tumor survivors into both recreational and competitive sports.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Editorial Commentary: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Requires the Right Patient, the Right Dose, and the Right Time.
abstract: Quadriceps weakness is a persistent challenge after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. When used as an adjunct to rehabilitation, neuromuscular electrical stimulation can aid in quadriceps strength recovery. However, optimizing the clinical application of neuromuscular electrical stimulation requires consideration of the right patient, the right dose, and the right time. Volitional activation failure can limit adequate voluntary loading of the quadriceps, particularly in the early postoperative period. Although the evidence supports early neuromuscular electrical stimulation use when activation deficits are most pronounced, treatment should be guided by resolution of underlying impairments rather than postoperative time alone.

title: Being treated as more than a diagnosis: A qualitative interview study exploring patients' experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance in the management of tendinopathy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tendinopathy rehabilitation often involves exercise therapy and patient education. However, limited research has explored how patients experience and assign meaning to the guidance through which such care is delivered.
OBJECTIVES: This study aims to explore how adults with tendinopathy experience and make sense of physiotherapeutic guidance in clinical practice.
STUDY DESIGN: This qualitative study adopted a hermeneutic approach and employed semi-structured interviews with 10 patients receiving treatment for tendinopathy across various anatomical regions to explore their experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance throughout treatment.
RESULTS: From the patients' responses, two major themes were identified: "Meaningful guidance is built through trust, recognition, and individualisation" and "Purposeful guidance helps patients understand and manage the condition". Three sub-themes surfaced within each theme, and similar topics were identified among the patients' responses.
CONCLUSIONS: Physiotherapeutic guidance appears to be meaningful when it integrates relational and functional processes. While trust, recognition, and individualisation support patients' engagement, clear explanations and structured guidance facilitate understanding and self-management in daily life.

title: Delayed Extensor Apparatus Reconstruction for Post-Burn Digital Extension Loss in a Pediatric Patient.
abstract: Late sequelae of pediatric hand burns may include occult damage to the digital extensor apparatus beneath healed scar tissue. The digital extensor apparatus is a complex anatomical system composed of interconnected components that function together to produce coordinated finger extension at interphalangeal joints. Injury to this system may remain clinically unrecognized during acute burn management and present later as isolated extension loss despite preserved joint suppleness. We report the case of a 10-year-old girl who presented 2 years after a flame burn involving the dorsum of the left hand with inability to actively extend the index and middle fingers. Clinical examination demonstrated absent active extension at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, whereas passive motion, sensation, and vascularity were preserved. Overlying skin was supple, though scarred and variably pigmented. Radiographs demonstrated mild proximal interphalangeal joint subluxation of the middle finger without other osseous abnormality. Surgical exploration revealed loss of functional continuity of the digital extensor apparatus distally. Delayed reconstruction was performed using an ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon graft to restore coordinated extension. Temporary axial K-wire immobilization was maintained for 2 weeks, followed by structured rehabilitation. At final follow-up, the patient achieved approximately 80% recovery of active extension, enabling writing and functional grasp. This case underscores the importance of early recognition of occult extensor apparatus damage following pediatric hand burns to prevent functional disability. However, delayed reconstruction can still yield meaningful functional recovery when joint mobility and neurovascular integrity are preserved.

title: Cortical button versus suture anchor fixation in distal biceps tendon repair: a comparison of objective four-plane strength and functional outcomes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare four-plane isometric strength, function and complications between cortical button and suture anchor fixation in distal biceps repair, and to explore the influence of surgical delay.
METHODS: Twenty-eight men (mean age, 44.2 years) underwent single-incision repair with a cortical button (n = 16) or suture anchors (n = 12) between 2020 and 2025. At a mean follow-up of 46 months, we assessed isometric strength in four planes with a hand-held dynamometer (relative to the uninjured side), range of motion, QuickDASH, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score (OES) and complications. A sensitivity analysis included only patients followed for ≥ 24 months.
RESULTS: Mean strength was 93.8% (flexion), 100.1% (extension), 90.3% (supination) and 97.2% (pronation; median, 94.2%); all planes except extension remained below the uninjured side (P ≤ 0.016). Strength did not differ between techniques in any plane, also in the sensitivity analysis. Functional scores were high in both groups, with small differences in favour of suture anchors that should be interpreted with caution (MEPS 100 vs. 95.0, P = 0.022; QuickDASH 1.3 vs. 5.5, P = 0.046; OES 47.4 vs. 43.4, P = 0.069). Repair after 21 days (n = 6; exploratory) was associated with weaker flexion (85.4% vs. 96.1%, P = 0.024). No reruptures occurred; three patients (10.7%) had transient neurapraxia.
CONCLUSION: No significant strength differences were found between techniques, although the small sample cannot exclude clinically relevant differences and fixation was confounded with treatment era. A small supination and flexion deficit persisted after both techniques.

title: Adhesive and Antibacterial Bio-Based Hydrogel for Human Voice Recognition and Osteoarthritis Recovery Monitoring.
abstract: Conductive hydrogels derived from natural polysaccharides hold great promise for next generation wearable electronics owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, adhesiveness, and tunable mechanical properties. However, realizing amylum-based hydrogels with simultaneously high stretchability, sensitivity, strong adhesion and antibacterial performance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a multifunctional ionic hydrogel, marked as PAPC4 hydrogel, composed of polyacrylamide (PAAm), amylum and phenol-modified chitosan is developed via a one-pot synthesis strategy. The hydrogel exhibits exceptional stretchability (up to 1605%), short response time (16.1 ms), high optical transparency (96%), strong adhesion (43.2 kPa on PVC) and pronounced antibacterial activity. Cytotoxicity assays, live/dead staining, and subcutaneous implantation supported its biocompatibility under the tested conditions, while bacterial assays demonstrated activity against Escherichia coli. As a strain sensor, PAPC4 detected joint movements and throat vibrations during speech. It also recorded differences in knee movement among control, osteoarthritis, and treated osteoarthritis groups in rats. These results support the use of this chitosan-starch composite hydrogel in wearable motion sensing and rehabilitation monitoring.

title: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears in the anterior cruciate ligament-injured knee: Current concepts.
abstract: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears (LMPRTs) compromise load transmission and secondary stability in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-injured knee and may be missed on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This narrative current-concepts review addresses incidence, risk factors, biomechanics, diagnosis, classification, treatment, and outcomes, while distinguishing root tears from lateral meniscal oblique radial tears (LMORTs). Primary ACL reconstruction (ACLR) cohorts report LMPRT frequencies of 7.1%, 10.0%, and 12.2%; a mixed primary/revision cohort reports 6.6% and selected revision cohorts report 20.5% and 40.7%. These study-specific estimates differ in lesion definition and ascertainment. Contact injury, concomitant medial meniscal pathology, and increased lateral posterior tibial slope are recurring associations. Individual MRI signs have limited sensitivity; combined assessment and arthroscopic inspection and probing support diagnosis. LaPrade et al. describe root-tear morphology, Forkel and Petersen additionally consider meniscofemoral ligament integrity, and LMORT typing describes posterior-horn oblique radial tears. The systems overlap for near-root lesions and are descriptive frameworks rather than validated treatment algorithms. Selected stable lesions may be observed; repairable unstable lesions are generally treated with footprint fixation or side-to-side repair, according to anatomy and tissue quality. Repair with ACLRn is associated with improved patient-reported outcomes and high complete-or-partial healing proportions in selected series. Clinical improvement in ACL graft survivorship has not been demonstrated. Heterogeneous definitions, predominantly lower-level evidence, variable rehabilitation, and limited long-term comparative data, constrain conclusions about cartilage preservation and optimal treatment.

title: A mechanically active microneedle platform integrated with engineered exosomes for enhanced tendon-bone regeneration.
abstract: Functional regeneration of the tendon-bone interface remains a major challenge because early healing is constrained by an adverse inflammatory microenvironment and insufficient mechanical cues. Here, we developed a mechano-regenerative strategy that combines YAP-primed engineered exosomes with localized biomaterial-based delivery and active mechanical stimulation. Exosomes derived from a YAP agonist (PY-60) preconditioned TDSCs (P-Exo) showed enhanced uptake and promoted the osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, accompanied by activation of YAP-associated signaling and PI3K-Akt-related pathways. To improve local retention, P-Exo were incorporated into a ROS-responsive adhesive hydrogel, which accelerated fibrocartilage formation, bone ingrowth, and biomechanical restoration in a rabbit tendon-bone healing model. To address more complex repair conditions, we engineered a three-layer self-contracting microneedle platform for deep-tissue delivery of P-Exo with concurrent active mechanical stimulation. In an infected rat rotator cuff model, this system reduced bacterial burden and oxidative stress, promoted a reparative macrophage polarization and angiogenesis, and improved tendon-bone structural regeneration, biomechanical strength, and functional recovery. Together, these findings support a therapeutic framework in which engineered exosome signaling and active mechanoregulation act in concert to enhance tendon-bone repair.

title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Treatment of clavicle fractures in adolescents.
abstract: Clavicle fractures constitute 10% to 15% of all fractures in adolescents. Historically, adolescent clavicle fractures have been treated non-operatively. Although recent data in the adult population has led to an increased rate of operative fixation in the adolescent population, a vast majority of these fractures in adolescents can be managed conservatively. This manuscript provides an overview of the current standard of care for clavicular fractures in adolescents in the context of sports medicine practices. To achieve this, a nonsystematic search of computerized databases of peer-reviewed articles was conducted, and a critical appraisal of existing literature was subsequently performed. Middle third clavicle fractures are by far the most common type and a vast majority of these fractures can be treated non-operatively with a sling given the robust healing and remodeling seen in adolescents. Lateral third fractures are far less common but may pose a risk for nonunion according to adult literature. Medial third fractures are the least common type and while they are typically non-displaced, patients with posteriorly displaced medial third fractures must have concomitant intrathoracic injury ruled out. Additionally, timing of the injury relative to competitive season could play a role in decision making as surgical fixation of clavicle fractures has been shown to yield faster return to play times.

title: Sexual dimorphism in morphological predictors of upper- and lower-limb strength in adult rugby players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sex differences in athletic performance extend beyond body size, encompassing morphology-strength relationships.
AIM: To analyse sex-specific associations between body size and composition (body mass, fat-free mass [FFM], and thigh volume) and strength (hand grip strength and isokinetic knee extensor and flexor strength) in adult rugby players.
SUBJECTS AND METHODS: 84 players (42 males) were assessed. Body composition was measured by air-displacement plethysmography, and thigh volume was estimated anthropometrically. Strength was measured by grip (kg) and isokinetic knee torque at 60°·s-1.
RESULTS: Males were taller (178.3 cm), heavier (82.7 kg), and stronger (hand grip: 48.2 kg; knee extensors: 252 N·m). Females had a higher fat percentage (24.2% vs. 14.1%) and lower strength. FFM was the best predictor of peak torque in males (r ≈ 0.69 to 0.74); body mass correlated best (r ≈ 0.45 to 0.50) with peak torque in females. The hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio was, on average, 0.56 in both sexes.
CONCLUSION: Strength determinants differ by sex in rugby players. FFM is the primary predictor of strength in males, whereas body mass is more relevant in females. These findings support the development of sex-specific training methods to optimise performance and potentially reduce injury risk.

title: Evaluation of Barbed Suture in Side-to-Side Tendon Transfer Technique Using a Cadaveric Model.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: To evaluate the biomechanical performance and efficiency of a barbed, knotless side-to-side (STS) tenorrhaphy versus a traditional running cross-stitch STS repair in a cadaveric tendon transfer model.
METHODS: Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons (index, middle, and ring) from 5 fresh-frozen male cadaveric forearms (mean age 52.2 years) were harvested and randomized into 2 groups (n = 12/group). Each pair underwent a 3-cm overlap STS tenorrhaphy with either cross-stitch with a 3-0 braided polyester (Ethibond) or barbed running grasping repair with 2-0 barbed monofilament PDS (Stratafix). After 200 preconditioning cycles at 0.5 Hz to 10% strain (≤30 N), constructs were pulled to failure at 1 mm/s. Primary outcomes were ultimate load and stiffness; secondary outcomes included force reduction after cyclic loading and operative time.
RESULTS: All failures occurred at the repair. Mean ultimate load was lower with barbed versus cross-stitch (111.4 ± 26.1 N vs 166.7 ± 34.4 N; P < .002); stiffness was also lower (8.0 ± 2.3 vs 11.9 ± 2.4 N/mm; P < .0006). Displacement at failure was similar (~19-20 mm). Force reduction with cyclic loading did not differ (39% ± 11% vs 34% ± 16%). Barbed repair time was 27.2% shorter (199 vs 272 seconds).
CONCLUSION: Both STS techniques demonstrated ultimate loads substantially greater than the 15 to 35 N forces reported during passive motion and early active postoperative flexor tendon rehabilitation protocols; however, barbed constructs were approximately 33% weaker and less stiff than cross-stitch repair despite reduced operative time. Although barbed STS repair may have utility in select situations, running cross-stitch repair remains the biomechanical benchmark, and further optimization and clinical validation of barbed constructs are needed before broader adoption.

title: Hydrogels as drug carriers for cartilage repair in osteoarthritis: Applications and challenges.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent chronic degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodelling, synovial inflammation, osteophyte formation, and loss of joint function, resulting in significant pain, disability, and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Despite advances in clinical management, current therapeutic strategies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid injections, and surgical interventions, primarily provide symptomatic relief and have limited ability to prevent disease progression or regenerate damaged cartilage. In recent years, hydrogel-based drug delivery systems have emerged as promising therapeutic platforms owing to their excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, injectability, high water content, and structural similarity to the native extracellular matrix. These properties enable hydrogels to serve as effective carriers for a wide range of therapeutic agents, including anti-inflammatory drugs, growth factors, nucleic acids, nanoparticles, exosomes, and stem cells, while providing sustained and localized drug release within the osteoarthritic joint. This review comprehensively discusses the pathophysiology of OA and highlights the major molecular signaling pathways involved in disease progression, including NF-κB, MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, TGF-β, and JAK/STAT pathways. Furthermore, recent advances in natural, synthetic, hybrid, and stimuli-responsive hydrogels are critically examined, with particular emphasis on their applications in cartilage repair and targeted drug delivery. Emerging approaches involving nanotechnology-enabled hydrogels, gene delivery systems, stem cell-loaded constructs, and immunomodulatory biomaterials are also evaluated for their therapeutic potential and translational prospects. This review provides an integrated and up-to-date perspective on hydrogel-based strategies for cartilage regeneration and disease modification, highlighting their potential as next-generation therapeutic platforms for the long-term management of osteoarthritis.

title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.

title: 18-years Follow-up after Mosaicplasty in Adolescent Athletes with Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Elbow.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty is an established surgical treatment of unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions of the elbow. However, the information on the long-term outcomes is lacking. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic results after autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty in the treatment of OCD of the elbow.
METHODS: This prospective long-term follow-up study is an extension of previously published data on 10 patients treated with autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty due to advanced, unstable OCD at the capitellum from 2003-2007. Objective and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated including Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score, Quick-Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (Quick-DASH), Timmerman-Andrews Score, a Subjective Elbow Value, and Range of Motion (ROM). Radiographic signs of osteoarthritis were graded according to the Kellgren-Lawrence classification.
RESULTS: At mean 18 years (range 16.0-19.7) five patients were available for follow-up. Mean age at follow-up was 34.4, and all five patients were women. MEPS was a median 100 (range 85-100). Activities of daily life were mildly affected in two patients. Two patients had non-symptomatic osteoarthritis grade 1 and 2. Patients experienced a functioning and near-normal elbow.
CONCLUSION: The long-term results after mosaicplasty are encouraging, and we find it reasonable to recommend mosaicplasty as the surgical treatment in this group of female patients with advanced, unstable OCD lesions of the elbow. However, it is of concern that two out of five patients had non-symptomatic early radiographic signs of osteoarthritis at an early age. As this study has an inclusion rate of 50 % of the original cohort, attrition bias must be taken into consideration.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series, treatment study.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Subject-Specific Cardiovascular Signatures Revealed by Arterial Pulse Signals in Patients with Heart Diseases-Part II: Special Cases.
abstract: Aim: This study evaluates whether cardiovascular (CV) parameters derived from noninvasive arterial pulse signals can reveal subject-specific characteristics in patients with atypical CV dynamics. Methods: Seven special-case patients-including a heart transplant (HTx) recipient and individuals with bradycardia (low heart rate, HR), low dicrotic notch (DN), and intermittent arterial pulse waveform (APW) variations-were analyzed across three visits over the cardiac rehabilitation (CR) period. Radial artery (RA) and carotid artery (CA) signals, acquired using micro-fabricated tactile sensors, were processed using a single-degree-of-freedom time-frequency (SDOF-TF) framework to extract multiple CV parameters. The analysis focused on descriptive characterization of subject-specific CV patterns in individual patients. Results: The patients exhibited highly heterogeneous CV profiles. Individuals with low HR exhibited relatively limited post-exercise HR changes. Individuals with low DN morphology exhibited elevated lower-order harmonic amplitudes. Individuals with intermittent APW variations exhibited cyclic changes in APW morphology at rest and during post-exercise recovery. Although CV patterns at rest differed across individuals, post-exercise assessment revealed more distinctive individual-specific differences, including differences between individuals within the same phenotype-based case subset. Across all patients and visits, RA measurements provided more stable and interpretable subject-specific CV patterns, whereas CA measurements were more susceptible to motion artifacts (MA) and sensor noise. For individuals with intermittent APW variations, the CA signals exhibited extremely poor signal quality, limiting their suitability for physiological interpretation. Conclusions: The SDOF-TF framework enabled the characterization of subject-specific, multi-parameter CV dynamics in these seven special cases. The findings illustrate the potential value of arterial pulse analysis for the individualized characterization of atypical CV dynamics. Future studies involving larger patient cohorts are needed to further investigate these findings and establish their clinical utility.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Subject-Specific Cardiovascular Signatures Revealed by Arterial Pulse Signals in Patients with Heart Diseases-Part I: General Cases.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This study evaluates whether cardiovascular (CV) parameters derived from noninvasive arterial pulse signals can capture subject-specific physiological characteristics and longitudinal changes in patients with diverse heart diseases. Method: Arterial pulse signals at the radial artery (RA) and carotid artery (CA) of each patient were successfully recorded from all 18 patients using micro-fabricated tactile sensors. Signal quality was screened before analysis, and the accepted signals were analyzed using a single-degree-of-freedom time-frequency (SDOF-TF) framework. Key CV parameters, including time-based indices-heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), respiration rate (RR), and respiration modulation (RM), as well as harmonic amplitudes and normalized arterial pulse waveform (APW)-were extracted from measurements at rest and post-exercise across three rehabilitation visits in 18 patients with heterogeneous CV conditions. Longitudinal changes in CV parameters within subjects and variability between subjects were assessed. Results: Compared with a healthy reference, the patients exhibited heterogeneous CV profiles, with lower HRV in all patients except one with AF, who showed elevated HRV, and generally reduced post-exercise CV responses. Higher-order harmonic amplitudes were attenuated at the RA, while CA-derived APW measurements showed greater sensitivity to systolic upstroke slope. Marked inter-subject variability was evident in at-rest CV parameters and 5-min post-exercise responses. Longitudinal CV responses varied across rehabilitation visits, potentially reflecting multiple contributing factors. Conclusions: The 100% pulse acquisition rate supports the feasibility of the tactile sensor technology for pulse measurement, and the combined sensor technology and SDOF-TF framework enable quantitative characterization of shared and individualized CV patterns in cardiac patients and their post-exercise recovery, including time-based indices, harmonic signatures, site-specific differences, and interactions among CV parameters. These findings warrant further investigation in larger cohorts with appropriate physiological reference measurements.

title: From bouts to readiness to compete: temporal dynamics of stress, fatigue, recovery and monitoring-informed decisions in combat sports.
abstract: Combat-sport tournaments require decisions before responses to previous efforts have resolved. Detecting a change does not establish that an indicator predicts the next task or improves a decision. This Perspective proposes a task- and time-specific framework linking prior bouts, recovery time and subsequent demands through three evidentiary requirements. Responsiveness concerns reproducible changes beyond measurement error when an indicator represents a response to effort. Predictive validity concerns anticipation of a pre-specified subsequent outcome and added information beyond simpler measures. Decision utility concerns improved outcomes relative to usual practice. Indicators interpreted as current status or stable capacity need not respond to prior effort, but still require adequate measurement properties and prospective evaluation. Evidence from repeated bouts, recovery interventions, mental fatigue, sleep restriction and weight loss suggests that monitoring domains are not interchangeable. The framework retains discordant indicators, evaluates combinations and communicates uncertainty without global clearance labels. Three hypotheses address task and time dependence, maintained performance with increasing effort cost, and indicator-informed decisions. Medical decisions remain independent and take precedence. This is an operational extension of existing principles, not a validated predictive tool.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.
